speakeroldname: Hon. L. B. Pearson (Leader of the Opposition):
subtopic: MR. PEARSON    REFERENCE TO REMARK IN DEBATE BY PRIME MINISTER
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I am raising a question of personal privilege arising out of a statement made by the Prime Minister in the house on Friday as reported in Hansard at page 3135. I have just had an opportunity of comparing that with the statement as it actually appeared in the press release issued by my office as to what I did say. The Prime Minister was quoting from a statement I made in Toronto on defence policy and he said:
I quote:
'Canada should contribute to the strategic nuclear deterrent."
At the time, Mr. Speaker, I raised the question that this was a misquotation. I asked the Prime Minister if he would read again the paragraph from which he was supposed to be quoting. Since that time, Mr. Speaker, I have had a chance of reviewing the text released and from which the Prime Minister was quoting. The Prime Minister only omitted one word, Mr. Speaker, from the sentence in question, but it was an important word. He omitted the word "not". The statement I made read "Canada should not contribute to the strategic nuclear deterrent".

speakeroldname: Hon. W. G. Dinsdale (Minister of Northern Affairs and National Resources):
speakerposition: Minister of Northern Affairs and National Resources
subtopic: NORTHERN QUEBEC
subsubtopic: ANNOUNCEMENT OF FINDING OF MISSING AIRCRAFT
speechtext:
I am sure the members of the House of Commons and Canadians everywhere will be profoundly thankful at the good news that the Norseman aircraft, which was the object of so wide a search between Payne bay and Fort Chimo in Arctic Quebec, has been found and that all eight people aboard are well and now safely at Fort Chimo.
Some further details have reached us in which the house might be interested, Mr. Speaker. The pilot's name is Paul-Joseph Garon. There were six Eskimos on board and the northern administrator, Mr. A. F. Flucke. The Eskimos were Mrs. Lizzie Unga Kauki, who was 67 years of age; Mrs. Susie Kudluk, 49 years of age and her children, Jonas, 17, Marcussie, 14 and Victoria, 12; and Miss Mary Adlook, 35.
Word of the whereabouts of the downed aircraft was brought to Fort Chimo shortly before eight o'clock last night by the pilot of the aircraft and a young Eskimo, probably 17 year old Jonas, who struggled into Fort Chimo after a 60 mile trek in blistering January weather to bring the news of the aircraft's whereabouts.
Savage winter weather has made communications with Fort Chimo unusually difficult since the R.C.A.F. search began, but we have learned than an Otter aircraft of the Quebec provincial police flew to the area of the downed aircraft and brought the party in. We know, too, that the Norseman had a good supply of food aboard, including a load of seal meat that the Eskimos were taking to friends at Fort Chimo, and that they built a snow house as shelter from the weather.
What started as a routine flight of a northern administrator going about his duties on a winter day has become a story of courage and resourcefulness in the best Arctic tradition. We thank all those who were active in the search which brought about this successful conclusion.

subtopic: * EFFECTS OF RADIOACTIVE FALL-OUT IN NORTH

maintopic: ERADICATION OF LAMPREY EELS, GREAT LAKES
ERADICATION OF LAMPREY EELS, GREAT LAKES
speechtext:
1.	What work is being carried out in lake Superior to eradicate the lamprey?
2.	What results have been attained?
3.	What work, if any, is being carried out in lake Huron and Georgian bay to eradicate the lamprey?
4.	What work, if any, is being carried out in lake Michigan to eradicate the lamprey?

maintopic: ERADICATION OF LAMPREY EELS, GREAT LAKES
speechtext:
1. The fisheries research board of Canada and its counterpart in the United States are involved in programs to eradicate the sea lamprey in the great lakes. Thirteen streams on the Canadian side of lake Superior and fifteen on the American side were treated with lampricide (a selective poison to kill lamprey larvae) in 1962. Electrical barriers are being operated in known lamprey spawning streams on the Canadian and American sides of lake Superior. In 1962 eight such barriers were operated on the Canadian side and twenty nine on the American side for the purpose of assessing the lamprey control program. Stream surveys to discover lamprey spawning streams were conducted on 178 streams on the Ontario side of the lake in 1962. To date 503 tributary streams have been examined on the south shore of lake Superior.
2.	Catches of adult lamprey at electrical barriers in 1962 showed declines of approximately 78 per cent and 82 per cent on the Canadian and United States sides of the lake from the averages of catches over the past five years. The rate of wounds and scars in lake trout catches in 1962 in lake Superior was 5 per cent or less. The 1960 wounding rate was from 8 per cent to 12 per cent.
3.	To date a limited number of streams on the Canadian side of lake Huron have been examined and treated.
4.	To date United States fishery agencies have surveyed 357 streams tributary to lake Michigan. Eight of these streams were treated with lampricide in the Green Bay area in
1962.

speechtext:
Mr. Chairman, may I, on behalf of the New Democratic party, take this opportunity to put our views before the committee with regard to some of the important

features of the legislation that the government has brought before the house in connection with the national economic development board. During the course of the debate members in all parties-I think some of them for the first time-have seen and acknowledged the necessity for the government of Canada to plan for Canada's future. I think some of the hon. members who spoke were late comers to this point of view, but we in this party are pleased that hon. members representing all parties in the house have spoken in support of the idea that Canada should plan her economic affairs and should plan ahead for her economic future.
All over the world countries have adopted the idea of social and economic planning. They are taking steps in the Scandinavian countries and in the countries of western Europe to plan their national economies to make sure that prosperity and full employment will come to their people in the days that lie ahead. Some of these countries have already achieved prosperity and full employment for their people but in Canada, due to the failure of the present government and its Liberal predecessor to meet the necessity for planning, Canada is declining. Other countries are flourishing while we are stagnating.
We in this party believe we have to take steps to adopt genuine social and economic planning. We have already expressed support for the legislation to establish a national economic development board, but at the same time we have advised the house of our misgivings regarding the form this legislation takes at the present time. We hope something can be done about that as we proceed to consider this legislation clause by clause, for we must adopt the idea of genuine social and economic planning. We must be prepared to establish a genuine national economic development board if the promise of material prosperity and spiritual fulfilment, which the twentieth century holds out for Canada, is to be realized.
I shall deal with one important aspect of planning that ought to be considered by the national economic development board, by the house and by informed public opinion. That is the idea of planning for the consumer, because when we talk about social and economic planning what we want to achieve is not necessarily the maximization of profit, not necessarily more and more production, but to provide for the consumer the goods and services he wants and needs.
Does the consumer today, under the economic arrangements we have, get the goods and services that he wants and needs? The consumer, the ordinary citizen-and all of us are consumers-is exhorted on all sides to consume at all costs. This is his sacred duty
National Economic Development Board to the free enterprise system. He is exhorted to consume all kinds of appliances and all kinds of commodities, but the question this committee ought to be asking itself is, does the consumer get what he wants and what he needs? I do not believe, and I do not think hon. members in the Social Credit party and at least some hon. members in the Conservative and Liberal parties believe, that our industrial machine is producing what people want and what people need. All of us are acquainted with the book that was written by J. K. Galbraith, "The Affluent Society". It is necessary to refer to only one of the examples he gave of the dilemma that faces the United States, and likewise Canada-the dilemma of public squalor in the midst of private affluence. He of course pointed out what should have been obvious to us, what should have been obvious to any administration that was planning the social and economic future of the country, in either the United States or Canada.
I think the most disconcerting thing that was revealed by J. K. Galbraith in his book was the fact that here on this continent we spend more on advertising than we do on education. Of course this leads to the question, what is more important, stimulating artificial demand for goods and services that the consumer may not want, that the consumer may not need, that the consumer may not have the money with which to buy, which may lead to his financial ruination if he tries to obtain them, or to provide that every citizen, every Canadian young and old should have the right to education whether it be technical, academic or vocational; the right to whatever education he can benefit from.
Even in terms of industrial development, even in terms of the necessity for expanding the gross national product, even in terms of the requirement of increased economic growth, it is essential that as we move forward into the age of technology, the age when scientific qualifications in many, many fields will be more than ever necessary; as we move forward into the time when our young people will have to be trained in all kinds of fields and will have to utilize all kinds of techniques that today we barely realize the necessity for, that we devote much greater expenditures to education than we are doing at the present time.
I was talking about the fact that the consumer must be given a place in the kind of planning that we have to adopt in Canada. We talk about the necessity for the consumer to have freedom of choice, and the members of the New Democratic party believe that the consumer ought to have freedom of choice. Economists today talk about the idea of economic sovereignty. Some of them say that

National Economic Development Board under our present arrangements the consumer has the right to choose whatever commodity he wishes to buy, and we do not wish to take that right away from him.
We believe that right is essential. We believe the consumer ought to have freedom of choice. But does he really have freedom of choice today in Canada? How can the consumer be said to have freedom of choice in an age of administered prices, when the prices he pays and the prices he is charged are not competitive; when these prices are administered by the people who control the large corporations in the key industries?
Last April we had as good an example of the fact that administered prices exist on this continent as we will ever have, when the leading steel corporations of the United States -by sheer coincidence-simultaneously raised the price of steel by $6 a ton. Of course this meant that the price of every commodity of which steel was a component would necessarily be increased by at least an equivalent amount. President Kennedy recognized the necessity for the government to intervene in the interests of the consuming public, and he did intervene and persuaded the steel companies to cancel the increase they had made. I think that is one of the best examples we can have of the necessity for planning for the benefit of the consumer, because that is what we are trying to achieve. We want to plan for the maximization of the choices that confront the consumer. We want to plan to make sure that he has genuine freedom of choice.
We in this party have advocated, on behalf of the consumer, that we ought to establish in this country a ministry of consumers' affairs. We have advocated the idea that in the cabinet there should be a minister representing the consumer, looking after consumers' affairs. We believe that such a minister ought to be a member of a federal planning board. We believe that the national economic development board should be responsible directly to the cabinet, not simply to the Minister of Finance. We believe that the Minister of Finance should be a member of that board, should be its chairman. And we believe that there should be a minister in the cabinet sitting on the national economic development board to represent the consumers of this country.
When we are talking about the necessity for planning for the consumer we have to consider how we can make sure the consumer has sufficient income to enable him to freely choose those commodities that he wants and needs. Of course we in the New Democratic party have advocated time and time again from this section of the house the necessity in Canada today for stimulating consumer


demand, for a planned increase in the supply of the money and credit, not an indiscriminate increase such as was advocated by the Social Credit party when it put before the house the idea of debt free money-an idea, incidentally, to which the Leader of the Opposition subscribed at that time. The Leader of the Opposition, in the debate on Friday, referred to the social and economic planning advocated by the New Democratic party as "magic nostrums"; yet the Leader of the Opposition advocated the idea of debt free money only a few months ago in this house, or at least his right bower in economic affairs, the hon. member for Davenport, advocated the idea of debt free money.
I suggest that it does not lie in the mouth of the Leader of the Opposition, who put forward that fantastically irresponsible idea, to denounce the members of any other party in this house as advocating "magic nostrums". I do not think the Leader of the Opposition had any clear idea of what debt free money involved, but at least his right bower in economic affairs should have known better.
We in the New Democratic party believe in the necessity for expanding Canada's social capital in order that additional money may be made available and spent. This may involve planned deficits; not the kind of financial chaos that this government has imposed upon the country, but planned deficits designed to enable municipalities, provincial governments and the federal government as well to increase the supply of social capital in this country, to increase the number of schools and hospitals, the number of community centres, to supply the country with the highways and bridges that it needs.
Mr. Chairman, we believe these things could be done, and in the process the number of jobs, the amount of money and consumer purchasing power would be increased, and the consumer would benefit because he would have the money to enable him to exercise genuine freedom of choice. We also need a countrywide minimum wage law to increase the incomes of consumers all over the country.
Let me point this out. Even if the federal government concerns itself with the necessity for taking all these steps to increase consumer demand, to give to the consumer sufficient income to enable him to buy the things he wants and needs, that will not suffice unless the planners, the federal government, concern themselves with the problem of interest rates. The necessity for regulating interest rates in this country should now be apparent to hon. members in all parties. It should now, I hope, be apparent even to the members of the cabinet. We already supervise the lending activities of the chartered banks; we already

regulate the interest charges which they make to the public. Surely it is time we got around to regulating the lending activities of finance companies, small loan companies, department stores and furniture stores. Surely it is time the federal government supervised the lending activities and regulated the rates of interest that are charged by these companies. It is necessary to cite only one or two statistics in order to justify the case for federal legislation to regulate interest charges in this country.

I appreciate the brief intervention you made in the debate, Mr. Chairman. Before my hon. friend the member for Bur-naby-Coquitlam and the hon. member for Essex East rose to speak on the point of order and to point out the relation between the regulation of consumer credit and economic planning on a countrywide scale, I was about to say that the amount of money which the people of this country owe to the finance companies, the small loans companies, the department stores and the furniture stores totals $2,450 million, while the amount they owe to the chartered banks totals $1,600 million. Thus the people of this country owe almost 50 per cent more money to these financial institutions, which now go unregulated, than they do to the chartered banks, which makes this problem a matter of great concern to economic planners and one which should be considered at an early stage by the members of the national economic development board when it is established.
Your Honour was somewhat disturbed lest I recite a series of examples of the imposition of harsh rates of interest upon members of the public. I did not intend to do that, but I agree with what, I think, was implied in Your Honour's remarks, namely that these examples are so numerous that if we once began to recite them members in all parts of the house would have hundreds of cases to lay before the minister. I am sure all hon. members are anxious that the minister and the national economic development board should consider this problem at the earliest possible time.

National Economic Development Board
There are some general features attached to the imposition of interest charges which ought, in my view, to come to the attention of the board at the earliest opportunity. These financial institutions that I have mentioned use a number of techniques to increase interest charges to those who make loans from them and to people who buy their goods far beyond any reasonable limit. There is the technique of not quoting the rate of interest, of simply telling a consumer that he is buying for so much down and $10 a month. There is the device of the added rate. A consumer is told he is paying, say, an interest charge of $6 on $100 over a period of one year, which sounds as if he were paying only 6 per cent. In fact, because he will have paid off at least half of the debt at the end of six months, he will be paying 12 per cent. There is the technique of the discount rate. A consumer receives $94 and then has to repay $100. This sounds like an interest rate of 6 per cent, but it is really 12 per cent. Then there is the simple monthly rate, which is what the department stores use in their revolving credit plans. The consumer pays 11 per cent a month, which is actually 18 per cent a year. A consumer may pay 3 per cent a month to a small loans company. That is 36 per cent a year. These are all aspects of the problem of excessive interest charges, and the national economic development board ought to consider the whole question as one of urgency.
We in this party believe there must be legislation to curb the exaction of excessive interest rates and to restrict interest charges to reasonable limits. We do not go so far as to advocate the idea of debt free money. I know this is one of the sacred policies of the Liberal party, one which they espoused with a good deal of vehemence last fall and one which the hon. member for Davenport and the hon. member for Essex East expounded to the house with their usual eloquence.

Nevertheless some of us were not persuaded that debt free money is a sound policy. We in this party believe we ought not to adopt policies such as debt free money, a policy which has been rejected by every reputable economist. We believe we should rely on policies which will commend themselves to people versed in economic affairs and who have some knowledge of sound economic and fiscal practices.
One of the policies which does commend itself to people who are knowledgeable in this field is a policy of regulating excessive interest charges and limiting interest charges

to reasonable levels. That is what this party believes in. We believe that this is a measure that the national economic development board ought to consider. This is a measure which justifies, in fact commands, legislation at the earliest possible moment by this government, or by any government which may succeed it. We believe that the consumer ought to be protected. We believe that legislation to regulate interest charges is one of the essential ways in which this protection can be afforded him. That is why, as the chairman of the committee quite rightly pointed out, some members have submitted bills to regulate interest charges. I myself, Mr. Chairman, have submitted such a bill.
Mr. Chairman, let me conclude my remarks by saying that the earlier the ministry, the earlier that this house, and the earlier that the national economic development board give their attention to the problems of the consumer, the better. When we are planning our economic affairs we are seeking to provide for the consumer the goods and services which he wants and which he needs. When we talk of planning we are concerned about maintaining a level of income which will enable all Canadians to purchase the good things which ought to be available to every one of them. We can do this only if we are prepared to regulate not only the supply of consumer credit, but also interest charges. Otherwise, if we took steps to increase the level of consumer credit-

Mr. Chairman, as the hon. member for Burnaby-Coquitlam has quite rightly pointed out, what we need is money which will buy something, money which will maintain its buying power. If hon. members do not yet realize this they should, but the policies advocated by the party of the hon. member who asked me the question are such that if we adopted the idea which they share with the Liberals, or debt free money, the result would be a galloping inflation in this country. If we accepted the magic nostrums put forward by the hon. member for Davenport, the savings of old age pensioners and the savings of other people on fixed incomes would be wiped out. There would not be any prosperity for anybody then. You must plan your economy. Increasing the money supply and increasing the supply of credit is only one of the economic tools which ought to be used when planning your economy.
Mr. Chairman, I was in the process of concluding my remarks when the hon. member was good enough to interrupt me and enable me to prolong them. We intend to do our best to make sure that that policy is adopted in this parliament.

Thus it is that, in a few days, we shall be called upon to vote interim supply, eleven twelfths. To my knowledge, it shall be the first time in the history of this house since confederation that such a measure is put forward.
Newspapers are devoting a lot of space to the difficulties now facing the government. Having had to delay until now its requests for funds, it has been wondering how to get out of this fix.

I was discussing indicative planning, Mr. Chairman. What interests me in indicative planning is the goal that is usually pursued. As you are aware, the French government at the end of the war developed the


Monnet plan. And in 1958, a French author named Pierre Bauchet wrote a very interesting book, entitled; "The French experiment in planning". I would like to quote two lines from that book to show you what, to my mind, is the main objective of planning.
On page 21 of the book I just mentioned, it says:
A concern for full employment Is, indeed, one of the essential motives for planning.
Now, I am surprised that in this bill there should be no section aimed at full employment, because the unemployment situation is alarming in Canada at this time.
May I refer to the latest report of the dominion bureau of statistics on the labour situation since 1962, where it is said that on December 15 there were 414,000 people without jobs.
Now, government members may declare loudly that our economy has improved in 1962, but the fact remains that 414,000 Canadians were without jobs. The figure is excessive. In fact, it means 6.3 per cent of the labour force. Now, 6.3 per cent of the labour force means the highest unemployment rate among the NATO countries.
I shall now quote from a document which was published in September 1962, under the title:
(Text):
"Report of President's committee to appraise employment and unemployment statistics, U.S. government printing office."
(Translation):
Figures are given, on page 235, concerning the unemployment situation in 1960, and it can be seen that the figures for December 1962 do not differ very much from those given for Canada in 1960.
In the United States, unemployment represented 5.6 per cent of labour; in France, 1.9 per cent; in Western Germany, 1 per cent; in the United Kingdom, 2.4 per cent; in Italy, 4.3 per cent; in Sweden, 1.5 per cent and in Canada, 7 per cent in 1960 and 6.3 per cent in December 1962.
The level of unemployment is still high in Canada. But, and this is more serious, unemployment is not of the same extent throughout all areas of this country.
I believe that is one of the causes of uneasiness that is felt in many areas of the country.
To support my contention, I should like to put forward a few figures. For December, in the whole of Canada, the figure was 6.3 per cent.

National Economic Development Board
If we look at the statistics for the different provinces or areas, we see that unemployment affects 11.6 per cent of the labour force in the four Atlantic provinces; 8.4 per cent in the province of Quebec; 3.9 per cent in Ontario; 4.5 per cent in the prairies; 7.7 per cent in British Columbia.
There is therefore undue unemployment throughout the country, but it is more acute in certain areas and very acute in the province of Quebec.

speechtext:
I shall come back to this aspect of the situation in a moment when I deal with the co-operation that is necessary between the federal and provincial governments.
I was speaking of unemployment and I believe that it is extremely revealing to consider at the same time the personal income per capita. Here we notice differences that are still more substantial. On page 38 of the last report released by the dominion bureau of statistics and entitled "National account, income and expenditure, 1961", we find figures for the personal income, per capita, in 1961.
If I mention these differences as between the various areas, it is because I shall later on insist on the importance of regional planning in a national economic development board with indicative planning. In Ontario- and this will certainly interest my hon. friends from the opposition sitting on my left-in 1961, the personal income per capita was $1,829; in British Columbia, $1,809; in Alberta, $1,582; in Manitoba, $1,476; in Quebec, $1,332; in Nova Scotia, $1,191; in Saskatchewan, $1,184; in New Brunswick, $1,054; in Prince Edward Island, $952; and in Newfoundland, $904.
Now, I notice that there is a difference of $497, or 37 per cent, in the personal income per capita between Quebec and Ontario.
Thus, I do not wonder why discussions are going on in the province of Quebec whereby people are questioning our whole participation within confederation. When we realize that our people are in an inferior position as regards unemployment, personal income, civil service, big companies-privately owned and crown corporations-we wonder whether
the economic situation is not mainly responsible for this attitude taken by the population of Quebec on its relations with the rest of Canada. That is why I believe that a national economic development board, at the federal level, is very important as long as it is well directed or organized, and has definite purposes. We cannot be satisfied with a body which will only collect statistics or wait until the minister directs it to make certain inquiries.
On the contrary, we must have a body bent on co-operating with the economic councils in the provinces, a body which will be concerned with regional development and production, which will envisage a full employment policy, the goal of indicative planning, as I mentioned earlier.
Indicative planning is easy to establish. We might very well provide for this in the bill, and I am certain that the whole Canadian people would welcome it. We should set up a working committee which would consult the various groups interested in production, the various professional groups which would submit reports pointing out to the Canadian government the objectives we are able to reach. For instance, there is in France a research body called the Monnet plan, which is composed of 90 people at the most. Those 90 people consult nearly 4,000 leaders of organizations, economists, labour union leaders, representatives of management and farmers' unions before suggesting the objectives to be reached within a certain period. When everybody is in agreement with regard to those objectives, the plan is submitted to the French parliament and means of reaching the proposed objectives are suggested. If it is impossible to so so by agreement among the interested people, no intervention on the part of the government could force them to reach those objectives.
There is also in France what is called government incentives, as we have them in Canada, but without any planning. For instance, for quite a long time the government has been subsidizing the gold mines, the transport of coal, and the transport of wheat from west to east. Grants are handed out without any co-ordinating policy. The government might very well resort to fiscal and other incentives and give priority to certain industrial areas.
To my mind, we could use such indicative planning in this country. For instance, I see no reason why we might not all agree on the objectives to be attained. I am convinced that
3170	HOUSE OF
National Economic Development Board all members in this house will admit that there is no valid reason for such a high unemployment rate in this country.
If we want to fight unemployment, we must agree on the means to do so effectively. As I pointed out a few moments ago by quoting some figures, unemployment is not the same throughout Canada. We might therefore try to favour some areas or some industries, so as to enable them to increase their production, in order to check unemployment in those districts. We have to promote full employment by all means, as well as co-operation between the various provinces and the federal government in the field of public investment. Every year the federal government as well as the provincial and municipal governments spend considerable amounts while there is no co-ordination between the various levels of government in investment matters.
Governments often act simultaneously on the labour or material markets, thus creating a temporary artificial scarcity. The federal government, the provincial governments and the municipalities do their borrowing without getting together to co-ordinate their borrowing policy.
It should be possible, within the proposed board, to plan government expenses in the field of capital expenditures, to organize planned government borrowing at federal and provincial levels.
This bill is based on the assumption that what is good for private enterprise or for individuals, is good for the community as a whole.
That is the famous saying which a former president of General Motors used when he said a few years ago:
(Text):
What is good for General Motors is good for the United States.
(Translation):
Now, that is a philosophy with which I totally disagree. The common good is not an aggregate of what is good for particular groups. We could all be very happy on our street and keep our door-step clean, but that does not mean that the sidewalk will be in the same condition throughout, that the garbage placed outside our door will not bother our neighbours.
I have always been amazed to find that the intervention of the government in certain fields has been accepted without discussion, and most particularly in postal matters, health, transport, communications, radio,

television and highways, and when it is a matter of national economic growth, instead of taking steps to fight unemployment or to develop certain underdeveloped areas, the government should retire behind the screen of "laissez-faire".
However, during the last war means were found to co-ordinate the efforts of the nation as a whole, in order to achieve a specific objective: victory. I am still wondering why, in peacetime, means can not be found to reach the very specific objective of full employment.
Of course, a bill like the one now under consideration is a beginning, a starting point. In fact, we are now on the way to an indicative planning policy, which is very well explained in the excellent paper issued by the national productivity council, entitled "Report of the European Mission". This booklet makes extremely interesting reading, and I wonder why the government has not drawn on that report to draft its own bill. It seems very well established that the members of that mission came back from Europe impressed by the indicative planning program in operation in the European countries they visited. Here is what we find in paragraph 24 of the said report:
All countries visited admit the necessity of planning, under one form or another. Most countries make use of "indicative planning" as one of the measures most likely to ensure economic growth.
Mr. Chairman, I feel that when we come to the consideration of the various sections the bill could be amended, so that when parliament has adopted it we may all rejoice, both members of the government and those of the opposition, at the very extremely important move which will finally ensure this country a policy of full employment, a decrease in unemployment and better relations between all Canadians, which we all desire and hope one day will be achieved.

Mr. Chairman, that is a very important bill because in my opinion it very definitely affects the life of the communities which I represent. However, in reading it I am surprised to find it only goes to the extent of providing a board which will collect information and make it available to the minister. If there is going to be any advantage from national economic development, what we need is a board that will be able to advise the government and provide it with the knowledge requisite for the formulation

National Economic Development Board
of a policy that the government can implement for the areas that are selected, either by the government or the board, for specific attention.
This idea has been adopted by governments all over the world. I have been very impressed, speaking to people like George Cadbury who has been attached to the United Nations, to find that the United Nations has sent officials to places like Ceylon, Jamaica and other newly developing countries to establish councils to advise their governments of the potential wealth of their countries and how to get the most out of national economic development.
We in Canada are faced with many major problems, and I do not make any bones about the fact that I do not expect the government, through this bill, will solve those problems. However I hope and believe they can be solved. I have no more faith in this government than I had in the Liberal regime which, it must be said, had a bureaucracy established that would have been able to undertake this type of work without such a board, if it so desired. Now, with a government that cannot run its own affairs, that finds us on a Monday, only a few weeks from the end of the financial year, without the supply motions necessary to allow us to discuss the business of the house in an orderly fashion, I cannot expect such a government to be able to take the advice of this board and put it into effect in order to establish economic equality across Canada.
The government has so little faith in this type of thing that it has brought forward a bill to apply to the Atlantic provinces. Why does it do this? To some extent, like the government, we are representative of the provinces and the provincial governments. The former speaker mentioned that in the province of Quebec this has been a great problem and that there were problems of a national nature in Quebec that were going to be aided by this particular bill. This is true of all the provinces, and it may be the reason for the introduction of the bill providing for an Atlantic development board, with stronger provisions than this bill. It may be that the provinces, the provincial governments and people generally throughout Canada are not yet ready to provide the government with the machinery that would establish an economic development council to provide full employment for all the people. It may be that they are not ready to support a bill which would provide the machinery necessary to make the most use of the wealth we have and achieve reasonable economic development in all parts of the country, using the wealth of the country.
We are particularly concerned with this in my area. We have built numerous communities on the strength of the basic resources of this nation. Many of our towns are only celebrating their semi-centennial this year. Many of them were very progressive in their day. One has only to drive through the town of Cobalt to know this. The people there talk of the days when there were electric railways running throughout the silver area, from Cobalt to Haileybury and New Liskeard, and from Cobalt into the Kerr lake camp. All these towns were further developed 40 years ago than they are today. It seems to me a shame that the people of those communities should find themselves going backward instead of forward, with their only hope lying in this type of development.
It seems to me the time has now arrived when we should not any longer be taking people to industry, like we still are in many of our larger cities, but that we should take industry to the people and to the communities that have already been developed. I am not suggesting this is the only thing we should be doing, but it is one of the first things we ought to do.
Why was it necessary in countries like Sweden, France, and most of the major countries of Europe? I would suggest it has been necessary because the free enterprise system works only on the principle of building up profits rather than on the establishment of economic welfare for the people as a whole. I think this has been recognized by many countries throughout the civilized world, and it is now being recognized in a small, token way by the government of Canada and the people of Canada.
It is surprising what favourable steps governments will sometimes take, but eventually they do take these steps. It is also surprising that these steps should be taken by a Conservative government, when one considers the fact that the Liberal party suggested they are to the left of the present government. I was surprised to read in Saturday's newspaper that in the province of British Columbia a Conservative government was suggesting a medicare program for the province.

The Conservative party. The Conservative government that is in power there has not got around to implementing such a program but I suggest this is only a matter of time; it also will make the same suggestion before the next provincial election.
One of the major things with which we should be concerned, apart from relocating industry, is the development of an economy
3172	HOUSE OF
National Economic Development Board for Canadians by Canadians. Many times I have been shocked by the control exercised by countries not under our jurisdiction but working within our boundaries. Not only is this work done by corporations of other countries but even sometimes governments of other countries.
I believe we are going to be advised in the next few months that we will be regulated to some extent in our economic development by what happens south of the border in relation to agricultural products. It has been suggested that if the United States, through legislation in that country, decides to scrap the present support program in regard to wheat, one of Canada's major developments will be in jeopardy, and rather than producing $2 wheat they will be producing $1 wheat. I wonder where our average of $1.50 will go if this happens. There is very little we can do about it in the present circumstances, and it seems to me that if a national economic development board is going to meet the needs of the Canadian people we must be in a position to do something about it.
On many occasions we have heard from and met with representatives from the automobile industry in this country. This seems to me to be a wonderful opportunity for the hon. member for Essex East to rise in his place and demand Canadian government assistance for an industry which should be Canadian. It is well recognized that it is rather foolish to buy cars that are manufactured for desert conditions and for conditions very unlike those in northern Canada; it is foolish to pay money for a product that is not meeting our needs. It is in the interests of the Canadian government to give some assistance to developing a product that will meet the needs of Canadians, and will meet them by the establishment of an industry that will produce something that is good for Canadians.
We must always be shocked-certainly I am always shocked-to hear that because of legislation or regulations passed in another country we are stymied in our economic development in this country because of our limited ability to sell the product which we manufacture. I refer to the Ford situation where Canadian firms were not able to sell to one country because it was considered not to be in the interests of another country.

subtopic: PROVISION FOR DEFINITION OF DUTIES, APPOINTMENT OF MEMBERS, ETC.
speechtext:
We in this party I am sure have no objection to Canada selling anything of a non-military nature to any country in the world which has the money to buy it or trade that can be used as barter for that product. We are a country that has to develop and we need to do so in an industrial sense. We can, it is true, increase our production tremendously in an agriculture sense, but at the present time we are not able to sell our present agricultural production. Industrially this country has a lower wage scale than many other countries throughout the world, and I believe we are in an advantageous position to go into the production of many, many other things. But I suggest that the economic development council would have to inform the government that assistance was necessary if this were to happen. We decided to sell food to Cuba, and we received a great deal of condemnation from several parts of the world for doing so. I believe that if the Cuban people wish to eat-and I think they do-and there is a product we can sell to them and they have one which they can sell to us, then we should do that and we should not care whether it suits the needs of someone else's economic blockade because they lost one of their little corporations.
I believe this is something Canadians have to do. That is why I am so shocked every time I hear a Liberal spokesman rise in this house and defend the right of another country to have some control over our corporations.

I think the Ford example is a good one to think about, because we have all met delegations from the automobile industry which have informed us that a great many of the employees of their industry are unemployed because no expansion is taking place in the automobile industry in Canada, and yet more cars are being sold in Canada every year. I think this is one of the things to which Canadians should give consideration. I believe that this domination of capital from other countries may make it necessary for the federal government to get into the field of supplying capital to industry in those areas that need it.
I have always been very pleased and very proud of the fact that the maritimes, an area which I agree needs development as badly as any other area in Canada, have on their own, without government assistance initially, developed the idea of industrial estates. I am pleased that the federal government, through the Atlantic economic council bill, gave some assistance to the idea of establishing industrial estates in the provinces of the maritimes. I suggest that this right should be given to the rest of Canada. If the rest of Canada is not ready for it, then let the federal government give leadership in developing plans so that the people will know the advantages of this type of development and will assist in bringing it about.
We in northern Ontario have always depended upon our natural resources as the main source of our income. There have been several examples where these resources have not been utilized for the benefit of Canadians. Right now silver that is being produced in my area in very large quantities is being shipped to the United States for manufacturing and refining to the extent where it can be used by the Canadian mint. Then what happens? The Canadian government go to the United States and buy that silver back because we have not the guts and the gumption to put $500,000 into the refinery that we already have in Cobalt. This plant can produce the mint silver that is required by the Canadian government and the Canadian government would save $2 per ounce if we were to do that. It seems to me that we have a terrific love for a foreign country if we are prepared to pay them an extra two bucks for the silver we carry around in our own pockets. This government has not the ability to decide that this Canadian industry is worth saving and do something about it.
We are going to be asked in the near future to assist this refinery. When the refinery at Deloro closed its doors United States interests offered to smelt the silver that we were not capable of handling. We are now capable of handling it. We have this plant-
National Economic Development Board it was operating under very odd auspices until recently-and it is worth the federal government investing some money in it to see that it operates in Canada for the benefit of Canadians. The silver industry is no small industry. This can be readily ascertained if we bother to find out the quantity of silver that is being bought at the present time from the United States. I do not blame the entrepreneurs in the United States for dealing with Canada in the way they have, but I do blame Canadians for allowing this or making it necessary. We have near Kirkland Lake an area which is a good example in this connection. The town of Kirkland Lake itself is dying quite rapidly. Every year another mine closes down. Miners are being laid off and no industry is being developed in the area so that this particular area can continue its economic growth in co-operation with other areas throughout Canada. Yet we found last year that a United States corporation was willing to come into the Kirkland Lake area, establish the Adams mine and start a mining development on which they expect to spend $30 million or $40 million in the next two years. I thank them for doing something which Canadians themselves were unwilling to do, and in some cases incapable of doing. I think there is a terrific waste of our natural resources in allowing this to be done.
I know we are not yet developed to the point at which we can use the total production of this large and worth-while mining operation but I think we are in a position where we could put in a smelter and develop a degree of manufacturing of iron and steel in that area so as to make it a booming area again. It seems to me that this iron industry will eventually employ people in secondary industries connected with it to the number of 4,000 or more, yet we in Canada will only have 300 or 400 employees. Again, we are to be hewers of wood and drawers of water for Americans who have more foresight than we have ourselves. If this government wants to develop a worth-while enterprise, an iron and steel industry in northern Ontario would be a venture well worth considering and, since it is already in the embryo stage, it would not cost too much money to carry out.
The idea of relocation of industry has been adopted by almost every major, economically developed country in the world, countries which have a high standard of living as hon. members may check for themselves. These countries have decided that they cannot afford to enjoy the luxury of unemployment such as this country still thinks it can afford, but cannot. I think one of our major advances in this country must concern the development and diversification of our industry, and the
3174	HOUSE OF
National Economic Development Board diversification of industry must inevitably lend itself to government planning. Why should industry go into towns and cities in metropolitan areas where more is asked for a small business site than would be asked for a whole city block in less congested areas, which are already developed, with water, sewers and electricity laid on; areas where the municipalities would provide the land almost free of cost because they are anxious to have industry and willing to help to the extent a small municipality can? What assistance do such municipalities get from the federal government?
The Minister of Finance is interested in this bill and rightly so. He has shown an interest in other acts for the development of Canada. But I wonder if he has given real consideration to the relationship between this bill and the Industrial Development Bank Act. There are a number of small industries in my own area which have gone to the industrial development bank for loans only to find that no money is available. Eventually they got the chartered banks to lend money with respect to enterprises which the industrial development bank had declined to accept as security. For example, ten or 12 farmers were running a co-operative dairy. A second dairy was going bankrupt and they went to the I.D.B. to ask for a loan. They have a large modem building with a great deal of equipment and by adding the second dairy they would almost double the amount of equipment available. They were not acquiring the other dairy merely in order to expand but, as I say, because the other dairy was going bankrupt and the farmers would be left holding the bag if someone did not bail this concern out of its difficulty. The I.D.B. told these farmers that the building was not worth more than the mortgage they held on it. They were told that their farms and their collective value as citizens did not mean anything at all. The bank wanted to see everything in black and white. They wanted to be able to seize the building and recover the value of the loan if anything went wrong, ignoring the fact that it would be a dairy with farmers depending on it. Money could be lent only on the building itself. I believe the collective value of our citizens is important. I believe the collective value of our farm economy is important. In addition, I believe the value of our unemployed should never be forgotten. These are all matters which should be taken into consideration. The other day I was approached by a young man who had bought a dry cleaning establishment. He told me that money was not available to consolidate his mortgages. These mortgages were considered good enough to be collateral for the building and for the equipment he had bought. Yet


when he went to the I.D.B. and asked for consolidation of his debts it was no dice; the building was not worth enough, and that was the only thing they could lend money on. What kind of a development are we going to have if this is the way things are carried on? Suppose we ask for money to develop a mining venture and the only thing the company has are buildings above the ground? Is the I.D.B. prepared to help an industry of this kind? I doubt it. Unless we revise the bill before us it will not serve industry in any way whatsoever.
The minister does not need further statistics to be collected. We already have statistics available. What he needs, as we see it, is a national economic development council which will tell him where we can get the most in the development of Canada out of specific expenditures in a particular field at a particular time. The government must then decide to do something about it. It is not good enough simply to advise the Minister of Finance, because the Minister of Finance is in a difficult position always. He finds that when everything else is paid there is nothing left over, the same as you and I do at the end of the year. If we are to undertake our economic development on the basis of whether the Minister of Finance says it is economically feasible or not we shall find we shall never develop anything in this country because there will never be any money left over. Hon. members can ask the char staff and the messenger service what happens when it comes to getting down to the bottom where the money is needed the most. The areas where development is really needed will be neglected in favour of the larger centres. They will find there is no money available for them, just as the char staff and the messengers have found. There can be no doubt as to the necessity of guiding the relocation of industry. Areas such as metropolitan Toronto and London, Ontario, are already facing problems of access and transportation which were unheard of 30 or 40 years ago. Problems such as these could readily be solved by industrial planning but the remedies which are most appropriate cannot even be considered under the terms of the bill which is now before us.
There are occasions, it would seem, when industrial plants are switched to other areas without even economic reasons being given for the move. There was a small plant in a town in my own' area which moved to another town not very much larger. I asked why it had moved and was told that the president's wife did not like the society she found in the first town. That was the reason why the concern moved. It is surprising that a free

enterprise system can be so arranged that even economic considerations need not be taken into account, but that an action so important to employees and others can be taken merely on the whim of particular persons. Another company left the town where I live and established itself in the city of North Bay. The head office is there and the company has between 60 and 70 employees -not many, but still the departure of the company was a considerable loss. The reason given for the move was that the comptroller lived in Montreal and found it easier to go to North Bay than to New Liskeard. By its very nature the free enterprise system works severe hardship on people, and though this is usually done under the guise of economic interest it seems to me sometimes even this motive is badly bent.
The federal government can give important assistance to the development of this country. Much of the knowledge needed has already been obtained. We do not necessarily have to go to Europe to find out what has been done in the various countries there, though I think this would help. Also, I believe, it has been done on many occasions. I know that when a man engaged in the lumber industry in my area wanted to find out how he could get the most out of his factory for a dollar-and he was engaged in an industry where the efficiency was very low-he went to Sweden and asked them what they did. When he came back to Canada I do not think he applied the Swedish system. I think he used the education which he had to adapt it to the Canadian way of life, and he now has a flourishing industry which uses many years of experience gained some place else to adapt itself to the Canadian system.
I think that we have to apply this method not only to the field of industry but also to the field of transportation. The economic development of this country will be retarded for many years to come if we do not face and come to grips with a national transportation policy. In my own area transportation is always cited as the only reason why secondary industry cannot come into northern Ontario. People say that this means the transporting of raw materials into the area and taking out of it the finished product. Yet I have sat on negotiations with a large factory in New Liskeard, the Hill, Clark and Francis factory, which also owns Hallidays and has an interest in many other woodworking concerns across the nation. Yet this company manufactures doors and windows for Simpson's, Eaton's, for Hallidays, and for many other companies, and will ship the doors and windows from New Liskeard to Toronto, Hamilton and other areas. These other companies in turn send them back to New
National Economic Development Board Liskeard, pay transportation both ways, and yet sell their products for two or three dollars less than they can buy them in the first place from the factory. This is not a transportation cost. It has nothing whatsoever to do with transportation. This is just another bugaboo used by industry often reluctant to look at the needs of the people and finding this as another reason to give for centralization of industry, in spite of the many problems which centralization has had.
We do not want to be unfair to the urban centres of Canada. We are happy that they have developed as they have. But the representatives from these areas will agree that some of the problems they now face in their urban development, or in the renewal of their urban development, will be at the expense of all Canada. And we are going to be happy in developing them. But in return for that, I believe they have an obligation to help those not capable of helping themselves at the present time. It is not possible for the people in my area to help themselves, because the money in the hands of any small entrepreneur who would do the developing is not sufficient for the type of industry which will be self-reliant and will be carried in the northern areas. It is true that there will be some small industry, but what we need is fairly large industry to solve the problems which we have. I ask this not only for my area; I ask it also for the thousands and thousands of small towns and communities across Canada. For example, I think of those towns in western Canada which even now find their only claim to fame is a rural elevator. And the signpost on which they have their name, indicating that they are a rural station, is not disappearing. Why can we not provide those small communities with industry to maintain them and to see them grow rather than disappear? We should be proud of the heritage our forefathers in the west and in the outside areas of rural Canada left to us, and rather than destroy it we should try to build it up.

Mr. Chairman, I welcome this opportunity to say a few words on this bill. I note with some satisfaction that it is taken in the name of the Minister of Finance. I want to say at once that as far as I am concerned, and I think as far as most of the people on this side are concerned, I am of the opinion that it could not be better taken, both from the viewpoint of the minister's goodwill in doing something worth while for the country, and probably also from the viewpoint of his ability to do so. But I am going

National Economic Development Board to suggest, Mr. Chairman, that the bill as written certainly does not warrant the hyperbole of praise given it by the minister when he spoke at the introduction stage. No doubt it will be subjected to some amendments, which I hope the minister will receive, in order to give it the ability to produce something for the Canadian people. Because as the bill stands, this is nothing more than the setting up of a permanent advisory board to the government. It says that.
The question I want to put to the minister is this. Does he not have at the present time in the various departments of the government that type of advice and information constantly at hand? We are in favour of planning, because we have seen in other nations of the world the results of planning since the end of the war. While we note with tremendous interest the great progress which has been made in those countries, such as the European countries and in Japan, I am rather of the opinion that most of it has been the result of invention being forced out of necessity. They were in grave difficulties and have now come back at a tremendous rate.
Our situation in Canada is not like the situations of those countries. To apply the principle of planning in this country on the basis they have applied it in western Europe and in Japan would, I think, be a most difficult matter indeed. I think the minister is aware of that. But certainly the bill as it stands will give him nothing more than a group of advisers, and I think that there are already a great number of advisers in various departments who can supply all this information.
I am going to make special reference to the particular situation in which Canada finds itself in respect to world trade. I noticed with some interest that a portion of the bill had some meat in it. I refer to the duties and the powers for which it provides. I want to tell the minister that far too much of the bill is given over to the provision of the people who will be on the board. Also I notice that only the chairman is to be paid, and that is the intention. However, the duties and powers are very interesting. Clause 9 of the bill says:
It shall be the duty of the board to furnish to the minister all such advice and information as will best assist the government of Canada in furthering a high and sustainable rate of economic growth in Canada, the strengthening of Canada's international financial and trade positionand this interests me very much-
-and the achievement of the highest possible levels of efficient productionand so on.

subtopic: ASSISTANCE TO EPILEPTICS
ASSISTANCE TO EPILEPTICS
speechtext:
That, in the opinion of this house, the government should give consideration to the advisability of introducing legislation to provide assistance to epileptics:
1.	by requiring the federal civil service and industry at large to hire a fixed percentage of employable epileptics, as is done in the United Kingdom and elsewhere;
2.	by promoting with the provinces admission of epileptic children in regular schools on the same basis as any other children;
3.	by increasing the research work on epilepsy, and by contributing with the provinces to the erection of treatment centres (Foyer Dieppe) for male and female sick persons;
4.	by improving the conditions under which epileptics live, through a more active public campaign.
He said: Mr. Speaker, two years ago, when the estimates of the Department of National Health and Welfare were under consideration, I had the opportunity to submit to the house the very special problem of epileptics. Last year, I had put on the order paper a notice of motion, but the early dissolution of parliament did not allow us to consider it. Tonight I am very happy to submit to this house this question which I feel is most important and I do hope that I shall be able to go over the subject rather briefly so as to allow members of the other parties to state their views on the matter.
First of all, what is epilepsy? It is a disease much better described maybe by its negative effects than its positive effects. Generally, epilepsy is not hereditary, nor contagious. It does not make one sick or unable to work nor does it make one mentally deficient; therefore, an epileptic is not less intelligent than any other individual.
Epilepsy can be described as a disorder of the nervous system, a very complex illness with the brain as its vital center. It can exist as le petit mal or as Ze grand mal. Usually, Ze petit mal is the phase of the illness in childhood or youth.
And today, the question is asked? How many epileptics are there in Canada? We have no

statistics available, but according to the criteria usually accepted in the principal countries of the world which actively contend with that disease, it can be said that one individual out of 200 suffers from epilepsy. In Canada, it is generally recognized that about 100,000 persons are affected by epilepsy at various degrees. That is why it is so important.
Mr. Speaker, I said a while ago that statistics are incomplete or non-existent. As a matter of fact, epileptic cases are usually concealed by the parents, and they are not to be blamed entirely because they realize much more than others that in our Canadian society-and I would say that the same situation applies in almost every country of the world-the epileptic is discriminated against at school and within the community.
And yet, following the advancement of modern science, when the epileptic gets all the required medical and surgical care, statistics clearly establish that about 50 per cent are completely cured, that there is a marked reduction of attacks in some 30 per cent of cases and that there are around 20 per cent of cases for which medicine can do nothing yet.
Having said this, one can wonder what the situation is for the thousands of epileptics in Canada and what we actually do to help them. If we answer frankly, we must admit, I think, that we do nothing, or almost nothing, in the face of a tragedy that takes place under our very eyes.
Mr. Speaker, I want to try and describe this unfortunate situation and suggest, in the light of what is done at present in the world, some means of helping those sick people.
First of all, at school: as soon as the illness is diagnosed, the child is immediately asked to leave school. That is the situation in Quebec, as well as in all the other provinces, I believe. If there are honourable exceptions, I would very much like to know about them. It is obvious that if it is known beforehand that he is an epileptic, the child is not admitted to school. Therefore, unless his parents can afford to hire a private tutor, the epileptic child is, first of all, illiterate. He is kept away from school, from children his own age with whom he could play. Thus he grows up isolated from other people and quickly develops all the complexes that make his illness worse.
When the child becomes an adult, he has no future except unemployment, because the same discrimination exists with regard to the
27507-3-201
Assistance to Epileptics adult epileptic. And yet, nothing prevents the epileptic from getting married because, usually, the illness is not hereditary, but through neglect and lack of understanding, he is not permitted like other citizens, to take an active part in society. Those are, briefly, facts which can be seen every day, if one stops and thinks about the epileptic's problem.
In Canada, at present, there are only very few observation, research and guidance centres for epileptics. I know that the Dieppe Foyer performs an enormous task with meagre means. However, there again, only men are admitted and only a very small number of patients can take advantage of those facilities.
If we look at the other countries of the world, we find a large scale offensive against the effects of that disease.
In France, the St. Paul medical centre in Marseilles, the most modern in Europe, has developed a research bureau with substantial grants from the French government. Famous doctors from the whole world are fighting a real international fight against that disease. Examination of young patients allows for a well co-ordinated guidance and, where a complete cure is not obtained, the child at least, is guided in such a way that he does not become a liability to society.
In the United States, the epileptic foundation in Washington is leading the fight on the American national level. Research work is concentrated there, and its results are made known to the American public through tracts and booklets. This informative publicity is directed toward parents, school teachers and the public at large.
In Great Britain, a specific act of which I have here a copy, was passed in 1954, under the title "Disabled Persons Employment Act". In addition to research work being done in Great Britain, this legislation provides that epileptics may be employed by the British government and industry. It provides that, in proportion to the number of employees of a particular industry or in the civil service, the employer must, under penalty of offence and fine, employ epileptics for the types of jobs they can properly discharge.
In Canada, I believe the time has come to become conscious of this problem and to take immediate action in the interest of epileptics.
I would remind you that we now have nearly 100,000 persons suffering from this illness in Canada. Only in extreme cases can they obtain a disability pension which
3178	HOUSE OF
Assistance to Epileptics is not conducive to a solution of their problem. I am of the opinion that we should ponder the problem a little while in order to consider immediate measures.
What can we do? What action could be taken at once to allay and improve the conditions of epilepsy sufferers?
First of all, I shall deal with the most important problem, that of education and training of children. At the earliest opportunity, we should, in co-operation with the provinces, find means to educate epileptic children. Let us start by providing those children with the education which will permit them to take their place in our society.
In other countries, figures show eloquently that epileptics cling to education as if it were their sheet-anchor, and that everywhere they are making very remarkable progress.
Second, we should do something at once for epileptic adults. Today these people are without hope, while it seems that we do not care about them. I think we should do what was done in Great Britain, that is we should pass legislation providing for the employment of a certain amount of epileptics in the civil service and in private industry.
I believe that if a campaign were launched along those lines-and I imagine that the Minister of National Health and Welfare (Mr. Monteith) is quite often called upon to address certain clubs, such as the Rotary or others-that if the example came from higher up, all our businessmen and industrialists, who are generally very generous, were they placed before that problem, would react by doing their part to place some epileptics in certain types of jobs.
I therefore suggest two main lines of action: first of all, education for the young; and employment, in all cases where it is possible, both in private industry and in the civil service.
If we take such action, we shall have done much, we shall have demonstrated, above all, to that great number of sick citizens that we are beginning to look after them; we shall have done much also to eliminate that misunderstanding which unfortunately is too often prevalent among the public.
But there would be much to do. We would need in every province a medical research center where we could give vocational guidance to young epileptics and re-education to adults. I think the national health department could send observers on the spot to Washington, France and Great Britain where they could get acquainted with the most


modern methods of fighting that disease and its effects. The department should also inform the public about that disease and about what every individual can do to lessen its effects, by using pamphlets and booklets to appeal to the sympathy of our educators and of our people.
When it comes to epilepsy, it is indicated in some reports that medicine, in spite of all scientific developments, cannot do everything, and that lasting improvement in the state of health of epileptics largely depends on their living conditions at home, at school and within society.
I hope this debate will have contributed, at least in part, to the desired result.
