speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of National Health and Welfare
subtopic: ASSISTANCE TO EPILEPTICS
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, may I commend the hon. member for Maisonneuve-Rosemont (Mr. Deschatelets) for his very obvious interest in the problem of epilepsy, an interest which we all very definitely share with him. It is a problem that arouses the deepest sympathy of every member in this house and, I am sure, every Canadian. We would all like to do everything possible for the unfortunate sufferers from this unhappy problem, and to see that they are given every opportunity, as he has pointed out, of receiving all possible educational assistance as well as medical assistance.
There is, of course, this same concern over disabilities of all different types. The problem, as the hon. member himself has mentioned, is that many of the things he wishes to achieve are difficult to initiate at the federal level. The house knows that many of the matters which he introduces in this motion have traditionally rested in provincial hands.
In so far as labour legislation is concerned, the first item in the hon. member's motion, my own view is very much against the rigidity of the compulsory employment of certain numbers of epileptics. It seems to me that the promotion of sympathy and understanding for all disabilities, combined with increased attention to their education, is a much sounder and stronger approach than the technique of compulsion, which has major disadvantages. First, there is always a certain amount of resentment when anything is compulsory. This would be particularly unfortunate in the very area where the intention is quite otherwise, in fact the very real need is otherwise. Second, if there is a compulsory number, it discourages sympathetic efforts and attitudes towards the greatest possible co-operation with handicapped persons in the very particular places where they find the very best chances for adjustment.

In many countries it is thought that the introduction of a quota system can tend to downgrade the jobs made available to disabled persons, and that employers tend to provide the most marginal jobs just to fulfil the quota. It is thought in some countries that the full abilities of disabled persons would not be recognized by employers under a quota system, and further that the disabled person himself would have some feeling that he might not have been hired because of his own particular ability. A classic example of the quota system and the supplementary of designated employment is in operation in Great Britain. Under the disabled persons act, every employer who has 20 or more workers is required to employ a quota, at present 3 per cent, of the registered disabled persons, and the act also provides a register.
For the most part employers have kept to this obligation and there have been very few cases where actual proceedings in law had to be taken. However, the committee of inquiry on the rehabilitation, training and settlement of disabled persons, reporting in 1956 noted that although they received no evidence that the quota system should be abolished they had been made aware that in the Scandinavian countries the quota system was not favoured, on the ground that in time of full employment it was unnecessary and in a period of depression it was unenforceable. Furthermore the committee went on to note that from the evidence received although the quota system has been of some assistance to settlement officers in placement work, its main value has not been here but rather to the value given publicity among employers. The committee recommended therefore that the quota system should not be abolished in Great Britain, but because of the educational importance of it it is clearly the British view that this placement by expert officers is dependent on the goodwill and co-operation of the employer.
In all countries the trend seems to be away from compulsory provisions that can cause ill feeling and perhaps even result in the placement of the disabled in jobs that might actually prove dangerous to them. The emphasis must be on filling needs on an individual basis with particular regard to the skills and physical capabilities of the persons concerned.
Considerable strides are already being made and I do take exception to the mover of the motion when he suggests that very little attention has been given to the problem of epilepsy. I think I can show him that considerable attention has been given to the problem. Strides have been taken in the area of improving skills, particularly through 27507-3-201J
Assistance to Epileptics an act to provide for the vocational rehabilitation of disabled persons, recently passed under the auspices of the Minister of Labour. Under the terms of this act, in co-operation with the provinces the federal government is making it financially easier to assess the condition of a disabled person, find out the best means by which he can be guided to suitable employment and provide medical treatment or any necessary equipment. Costs are shared equally by the two senior levels of government and the program should have far reaching implications.
There are many tasks which can be performed well by disabled persons and I know the government is anxious to foster recognition of this, both inside the civil service and in industry generally. It seems to me, however, that there is still a great deal of public education to be done in this regard and there is still considerable reticence on the part of the handicapped themselves in admitting their problems and disabilities. This situation of course will be somewhat eased and improved as public education increases and sympathy thereby increases.
Much has been done and still can be done through large companies which have industrial physicians and nurses. There are, however, as we know, many small companies which do not have and may not be in a position to contemplate medical services of any kind in the near future. In this case general public acceptance and understanding of disabilities, including epilepsy, will gradually open increased employment possibilities. In this respect the Canadian epilepsy foundation, with its headquarters in Toronto, is doing admirable work, and such groups deserve every possible encouragement and support.
Within the civil service disabled persons are employed wherever their capabilities fit some particular position, and I believe that the federal government is giving a very strong lead in this respect. To require the employment of a fixed percentage would create many difficulties in terms of decisions as to who could or could not be hired, and where they could or could not be placed, and it seems to me this is very nearly unworkable in this country.
The hon. member speaks of the possibility of increasing the research work on epilepsy but here, as elsewhere, we run into the problem of provincial responsibility. The national health grants program was established to help provinces expand their own research programs and related matters, but decisions as to where the emphasis should be placed are made in the provincial capitals.
Since this government came to office it has increased the available amount of hospital

Assistance to Epileptics construction grants by 55 per cent, and other national health grants by 20.5 per cent, with a view to stimulating progress in all health fields. The Foyer Dieppe, which the hon. member mentions, has benefited to a considerable degree, in fact to the extent of over a quarter of a million dollars. Since 1957 it has received this total from federal funds, and indeed the federal contribution to the problem of epilepsy throughout the whole country has been $1,126,000. This has assisted epileptics throughout the whole of Canada.
Since the mover of the motion seems to feel so strongly that so little has been done, I might just break this total down. Foyer Dieppe has received in federal assistance, already expended or approved, the amount of $292,323; Hotel Dieu du Sacre-Coeur has received expended or approved federal assistance in the amount of $596,426; and the Montreal Neurological Institute $47,256.
In Ontario we have the outstanding epilepsy centre in Woodstock which has received federal assistance expended or approved in the amount of $149,452. In Saskatchewan we have the University hospital in Saskatoon which has received $8,713, and in British Columbia the British Columbia epilepsy society in Vancouver has received $32,406 for the employment of personnel for the operation of an epilepsy centre.
In 1953 the British government appointed a committee of inquiry on the rehabilitation, training and resettlement of disabled persons, and in 1956 they brought forward a very interesting report. On page 74 of this report there is particular mention of epileptics and it is interesting to note this statement;
The most important finding of the report is that recent advances in medical knowledge offer much greater hope that epilepsy can be controlled, particularly if they can be made generally and readily available through an organized pattern of specialist units... This means that it should be easier in the future than in the past for an increased proportion of epileptics to live a normal life in the community, whether as schoolchildren receiving education in ordinary schools or as workers taking a normal place in open industry. Clearly this should be the objective. There must, however, be some proportion however small, who will need special provision whether for short or long periods, in the same way as other disabled persons-for example, special schools, rehabilitation units, sheltered employment, residential hostels, etc. Their needs require also the same close co-operation between the different authorities responsible for the different services which the committee has emphasized elsewhere.
The Canadian government's attitude at the present time follows this recommendation very closely, as can be seen from the considerable amounts expended or authorized already, in the medical services towards helping epileptics in their physical improvement and development, and also in different types
[Mrs. Casselman.j
of rehabilitation training and educational assistance for those who are definitely handicapped.
It is my very strong feeling that there are definite dangers in seeking to establish legislative authority for one group of handicapped persons, with the very possible exclusion or neglect of others, however unintentional this may be. Circumstances change from year to year, and in general there is more to be said for an approach where the provinces are free to gear their programs to the needs of their own citizens and afterwards approach the federal authorities for the necessary aid.
Rehabilitation matters are of great significance in the whole general field of social welfare. This year we have seen legislative authority provided to establish a national council of welfare to advise the government on all aspects of the welfare situation. I would hope that it will turn its attention to this area of epilepsy and all disabled persons, and make suggestions as to how and where the government's present activities can be improved. They will thereby be adding to the already valuable advice we receive from the national council of welfare, and have been receiving for many years.
This morning I had the honour to welcome on behalf of the minister the federal-provincial conference of public health nurses. This is their second conference, the first being held in February of 1961. Representatives from the provinces are gathered here in Ottawa in a very impressive group. They are experienced in and deeply concerned with this important public service. This is another avenue, it seems to me, through which we will have increasing opportunities for assisting in all health problems, including recognition of the different types of epilepsy and advice as to how and where the best treatment and rehabilitation can be obtained for them. This growth of co-operation between different branches of government in any field is encouraging, and it is most particularly encouraging in the field of public health. I believe we can expect from this conference and subsequent conferences on public health nursing an increased understanding, an increased ambition toward definite, co-operative aims which will lead to very improved methods of dealing with this problem which the hon. member for Maisonneuve-Rosemont (Mr. Deschatelets) has rightly brought forward, and it will also include very serious consideration of the problems of all disabled Canadian people.

subtopic: ASSISTANCE TO EPILEPTICS
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I rise at this time to acknowledge our indebtedness to the hon. member for

Maisonneuve-Rosemont (Mr. Deschatelets) for bringing this matter to the attention of the house. As we consider the notice of motion that is on the order paper we note that there are some particular clauses regarding which we might raise some objection and some question, but I think all of us recognize the intent of this motion and feel that the hon. member has, as I have said, made a valuable contribution in bringing it to the attention of the house.
It seems to me that in the consideration of a measure such as this there are a great many other issues that might enter into it. The parliamentary secretary to the Minister of National Health and Welfare has referred to some of the problems involved. In her remarks the hon. lady has pointed out the possibility of discrimination-and I use that word advisedly-if we endeavour to make legislation apply to only certain classifications of our citizens. I would prefer to consider this in its broader aspect, not only stressing the importance of consideration for those who are suffering from this particular handicap but those who are suffering from other handicaps or disabilities which make it difficult for them to fit into the picture of employment across the country.
I believe some categories of our citizens are subjected to some form of discrimination in their search for profitable employment. I think that often this discrimination results from ignorance, but there are times when it is the result of economic considerations. Those engaged in industry hesitate to employ people who are suffering from various types of handicaps or disabilities because they feel there would be an interruption in service on the part of the employees which could result in a loss of efficiency as far as their operations are concerned. I think that research has proven this fear groundless. In fact, it has often been established that those who are handicapped in some particular way more than offset that difficulty by their devotion and diligence to the tasks assigned to them, which qualities may often be lacking in those who are not handicapped.
Therefore I feel that this word of exhortation might go out not only to governments but also to private industry, not to discriminate against those who may be handicapped in this or other ways, but rather give them an opportunity to engage in profitable and productive employment to the very highest degree of their ability and qualifications. I agree with the suggestions made by the parliamentary secretary to the minister in stating that it would be very difficult to set a specific percentage to be employed by the civil service, and I would once again emphasize the fact that rather than place it in that
Assistance to Epileptics particular context we would suggest that no discrimination be practised when it comes to a matter of the employment of employable epileptics and those who are suffering from other types of disability.
The question of the education of epileptic children is a very important consideration. Whether or not the suggestion made in clause 2 would be applicable in all circumstances is perhaps open to question. I would not be in a position to pass judgment on that particularly, except to say that I believe consideration would have to be given to individual cases and to the degree of affliction in this respect. Reference has been made to the matter of research and treatment centres. It would seem to me that this is a field into which the federal government could move in a very constructive manner. Once again the parliamentary secretary has indicated the contributions which have been made in this respect. However, I would suggest, Mr. Speaker, that as far as the provision of these facilities is concerned-that is, treatment centres and so on-our suggestion relative to the use of a municipal development bank would be very useful. Through the provision of social capital through the Bank of Canada we could make a greater amount of money available for the erection of these institutions and for the facilities which are required for the effective treatment of these people.
As I have said, Mr. Speaker, I rose only to indicate support of the principle or motive incorporated in this particular measure, but I suggest there should be-as there is, I believe-a growing awareness on the part of society to bear its responsibility in assisting those who are handicapped in any way, giving them the fullest opportunity to co-operate and participate in activities and make the highest contribution possible under the circumstances. We are, as I have said, very happy to give support to the motive and principle contained in this measure.

subtopic: ASSISTANCE TO EPILEPTICS
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, we of course support the principle stated in this motion. I have not had very much experience with epileptics, although as a teacher I can tell hon. members that a great many of them do attend the ordinary schools. Of course, it depends upon the individual and the degree of the infirmity, but many of them do attend schools. The teachers are simply notified that this person is an epileptic and in most cases there is no particular problem. The affected students fit in with the school pattern well provided they are not severe cases.
I have had experience with another type of handicapped. Of course, there are mental as well as physical handicaps, and for some years I was associated with the affairs of a
3182	HOUSE OF
Assistance to Epileptics home for retarded children in my own constituency of Burnaby. The type of handicap is different, but the problem of obtaining employment is the same. Another factor which must be considered is the considerable burden which falls on the parents. In the last few years the associations for retarded children in all the provinces have done a great job in making governments at various levels aware of the needs of retarded children. In my own province, governments, both municipal and provincial, have responded to these needs, after considerable pressure, by providing places in local schools or by providing special schools for these children. In my own province, after a number of years of endeavour, we do now have most of the retarded children attending schools at public expense.
The associations have now moved on and are trying to do something for adults and teenagers. Sheltered workshops have been set up which these people can attend and at which they can receive the necessary technical training. After a probationary period, they receive pay. They are not doing make-work jobs but are carrying out useful tasks. When companies want particular jobs done, the sheltered workshops do them and, in turn, pay the retarded adults who are working there.
It has always seemed unfortunate to me that there has to be such a vigorous program of public education before we make a move in these matters. The pattern seems to be the same everywhere. The people affected, in many cases the parents of handicapped children, have to form an association and carry out a program of public education before they can get governments to act. I would feel better if this country and those in a position of responsibility would recognize that these problems exist and do something about them before they are forced to take action. We know very well what our health and social needs are. We do not need to be told, in many cases.
There is one other aspect of this subject to which I should like to refer. I do not think we can divorce the difficulty which handicapped adults find in obtaining employment from the general economic situation. It is difficult enough for these people to get employment at the best of times, but when there are a large number of unemployed in this country it is still more difficult for them. I hope the day will come in Canada when we have a period of full employment and even a labour shortage, because I think it will be much better for these people at that time.
[Mr. Prittie.J

We cannot get away from the fact that it is very hard indeed for them to get employment.
The parliamentary secretary-and I congratulate her on having certainly done her homework on this topic-has spoken against the idea put forward in subparagraph (1) of this resolution, that some compulsion should be applied regarding the employment of epileptics. Unfortunately, I think this would be necessary in many cases because if there were not some compulsion very few would be hired. The hon. lady did answer a number of questions on this topic and I should be pleased if before this debate is over she would answer one other question. She said that the civil service, or the government, was employing a certain number of epileptics. I should like to know, if possible, how many are at present in employment. If this question cannot be answered today, perhaps she will answer it at a later time. However, I am glad that something is being done in this connection. The hon. lady also gave us information concerning the amounts granted to the various societies in the provinces for work in this field. I noted that $32,406 was mentioned in connection with the British Columbia association. I must say in this connection that it does not seem like a very large amount. Perhaps I might have some information on this subject as well: is this a case where more money would not help solve the problem, or is it all the money that is available as a grant at this time? The parliamentary secretary has pointed out that certain things have been done, and we are very glad of that. Nevertheless, the motion which has been put forward today does serve a useful purpose. It reminds us all of this subject, and although the department may be doing something there is certainly no reason for self satisfaction. I hope it will serve as a reminder, to bring this matter to the fore and keep it in the mind of the department.

speechtext:
As one
who is vitally interested in the broad scheme of rehabilitation I want to send a salute to the hon. member for Maisonneuve-Rosemont (Mr. Deschatelets) for bringing to public attention this frightening question of the problem of the epileptic. It is not confined, of course, to the epileptic alone, as has been pointed out by the hon. member who has just spoken; it is a problem which faces disabled persons generally. Somehow, however, the case of the epileptic is the most frightening because it is a shocking experience for people who are not in daily contact with epileptics to witness an epileptic seizure. It seems to me there is a terrific amount of prejudice and misunderstanding about this disease, as previous speakers have said. I myself, would question the advisability of singling out this one disability for special attention and for special legislation. However, the subject well merits discussion and deserves public attention to be focused on it. Modern society still seems to cherish some medieval ideas about this whole subject of epilepsy. The epileptic appears to suffer a double handicap; it is not only the illness itself but the prejudice and misconception surrounding it which he has to overcome before he stands a chance in the labour market. We are, of course, speaking of the employable epileptic.
I have wondered what could be done about rehabilitating other disabled persons and I was interested to hear what the hon. member for Maisonneuve-Rosemont told us about legislation in the United Kingdom parliament. I think he described it as the disabled persons employment act. I was, therefore, somewhat surprised to hear him centre his motion on the epileptic. I think he would have been better advised to have included other disabled persons as well. I think it is not feasible to guarantee employment by legislation alone. In fact, I wonder sometimes just how useful legislation can be in achieving an object which we would all agree to be desirable. Largely it is this question of public attitude which surrounds any disability. I think the hon. member has referred to the work done by the association of retarded children, just as other work has been done for people who have other afflictions. We need a public education program which will induce the public mind to consider people who are less than completely or abnormally physically endowed for various enterprises in the field of employment, education, research and so forth.
Assistance to Epileptics
One of the difficulties about the epileptic is, I suppose, the misconception that he is often less intelligent. I think that research would certainly bear out the fact that this is no more so than in any group of population which is physically normal. There is always a spread of intelligence. Largely the lack of knowledge in the epileptic is due to the fact that he has not the opportunities of education because in some areas and in some instances he has not been accepted in the schools among normal children. As far as the section of this motion which refers to including epileptic children in ordinary schools is concerned, comments have been made about this, but I would certainly question the advisability of doing this in toto. I believe that certain epileptic children would be better helped if they were at least in special classrooms where they would have the treatment they need if and when they were subject to seizures, and where they would not be perhaps subject to ridicule or much excitement by other children, were they unfortunate enough to have a seizure. Therefore I cannot quite accept the suggestion of the hon. member in the second part of his motion that measures should be introduced to admit children into ordinary schools. I am sure that on further elucidation he would say he meant that only in certain cases would this be so. The question of legislation is still only a secondary solution. I think the broadest improvement which could benefit any disabled person is to have a greater public awareness of the needs of disabled people.
When we speak of having concern for the individual rights of people-I think this is a phrase which we have heard in more recent times-we must not forget the rights of disabled people as well. Certainly these rights are denied if they have not been given equal opportunities of education, of employment, or even given accepted places in society as healthy persons with whom to associate. Sometimes they are so much isolated that they fear to be part of the normal community even though they could well find a useful place in the community. So that really more necessary, I suggest, than education would be research and vocational training. These facilities would require, of course, substantial grants from the government, and I think they would be forthcoming if they were submitted to the appropriate legislature, which I presume in most cases would be the provincial governments.
I also think there has to be a wide program of public education which would make the average person more aware of just how much these people can really contribute to our community. I think it is a mistake if we let people
3184	HOUSE OF
National Economic Development Board just live off assistance because they are disabled. This is certainly not the answer. There is in all labour some dignity, and anyone who is working wants to know that he is doing something worth while, and that he is earning his keep. Therefore, even if it needs to be a sheltered workshop, or a specialized centre for epileptics or other disabled persons, he needs to have some satisfaction in his work.
I feel that these are areas for private agencies who have already done so much to meet various human needs in our communities and to enable them better to develop. Because private agencies have a capacity for community involvement which is much better and greater, and are much more capable than any act of parliament. That is because they are interested in epileptics and form a group, a chapter or agency to try and aid the needy epileptics. In that way you are much closer to the problem and much more vitally and personally interested; therefore, the results are much more far reaching. Of course, aid is required from government finances. However, the initiating program I suggest would be best advanced by the widening of the scope of private agencies which already exist in this field.
It is to be hoped that all levels of the community and all levels of industry will examine and re-examine their employment practices where they can, and in that manner will afford to disabled persons, including epileptics, employment possibilities. This is necessary in order that the achievement of an elemental human right is attained-that is, the right to live and work in a normal way. I feel that the hon. member has done a great service to the epileptic by introducing this resolution, and the very fact that there has been this spirited and interesting discussion will be of benefit to all these disabled persons.

speechtext:
Mr. Chairman, at five o'clock I had completed my congratulations to the minister who is guiding this bill through the house, had made some comment upon the general condition of sterility in the bill itself and was beginning to pay some attention to the fact that one section of the bill deals with the very important consideration of paying more attention to Canada's balance of trade and trading position. It is with that particular aspect of the bill, which is designed to provide for the establishment of a national economic development board, that I want to say a few words to the committee tonight.
Last week a very important speech was made by a very important man. I refer to the speech made by Mr. R. M. Fowler which has now been published and which he has titled, "Wanted, A Trade Policy". It might well be argued that Mr. Fowler represents a definite segment of the Canadian economy but I think every member of the house will agree that he is a very well informed Canadian and a very able businessman, that his views should be listened to, and that the government of the day should profit therefrom. Inferentially he suggests that we do not have a trade policy, and he wants a trade policy. He wants a policy directed toward a definite objective for Canada today and in the future.
I think we might well profit from a consideration of the historic position of Canada in trade. In the early days of Canada and government in Canada I think there must have been a widely held opinion in this country that we could make some permanent long time arrangement with the country to the south. When that failed there emerged in its place the historic national policy of Canada and the name of Sir John A. Macdonald. Quite obviously the concept at that time was that the central provinces would manufacture goods for Canada which would be transported on transcontinental railways to areas whose raw materials would be sold, and the proceeds used to buy the manufactured products of central Canada. That policy served us in its day and we went on to other things.
In the period between the two great wars we built up in Canada the historic so-called

triangle of trade. We sold great quantities of goods to the United Kingdom and became very interested in commonwealth trade, particularly the advantages given us under commonwealth agreements. We took pounds sterling which were transferable very easily into our currency to enable us to buy tremendous quantities of manufactured goods from the United States. If you study the period between the wars you will find that is the trading history of Canada in that particular period.
During the period of the second world war tremendous demands were made upon Canada in the area of things which we were able to provide and manufacture and as a result of particularly good management we came for the first time to the point where I think we could consider ourselves at least in part an industrial nation. Now we are confronted with a new set of circumstances in the world where great trading blocs are rising and where agreements are being made not between one nation and another but between blocs of nations, and I think it is time now for us to inspect again the basic, fundamental problems that we have within our own country.
I come from a province which at the present time is selling to the United States $50 million worth of goods per month or about $600 million a year. About $125 million is represented by sales of energy in the form of oil and gas. We also sell $204 million worth of lumber per year. These articles are basically raw materials which British Columbians are finding command basement bargain prices in world trade, the lowest possible prices at which any goods are sold. At the same time that we are selling $50 million worth of goods per month to the United States, according to figures which are the most accurate I could obtain from our provincial department, though I would not say they are absolutely accurate, our trade with that old historic province of New Brunswick only amounts to about three quarters of a million dollars per year. When we look askance and are worried about great trading blocs and the common market, I think we must also admit that within our own country we have failed dismally to create a common market in Canada. This, of course, is a regional matter. I know that the minister is aware of the situation because I know I am aware of it.
I want to draw his attention to the fact that from Prince George in the central interior of our province we ship about $80 million to $100 million worth of lumber per year. Historically this lumber has gone to the head of the lakes and from there largely to United States markets around Buffalo. At the present time the shippers of this lumber 27507-3-202
National Economic Development Board are faced with the Damoclean sword of a threatened 17 per cent increase in freight rates, when the lumber is already bearing an impost of $34 per thousand to reach Buffalo. I think the minister will agree with me that if the railways were suddenly granted the 17 per cent to which they claim they are entitled, and this amount was added to the cost, it would be extremely doubtful that the lumber industry there could survive, and at this time I know of no other market for that particular grade of lumber.
These are conditions within this immense industry which have arisen out of our history, out of geography, and which we have to face. I think we should face them in a spirit, not of what we hope Canada might be, not what we see in other countries, but considering the development of Canada and in the love of Canada as she is and not what we might hope she is. These are difficulties with which we are confronted and they require, I would suggest to you, Mr. Chairman, a far different attitude on the part of our federal government than we have seen in recent months and in recent years. It gets back to this, that in these matters of trade policy which Mr. Fowler is suggesting, we must seek to adopt a policy for our own country which is intelligent, honest, honourable and promises respect in the various parts of this country.
I notice that in Ontario they have a man named Macaulay, who is making certain suggestions. It may well be that for the short term period they may be of advantage to the people of Ontario. However, I doubt very much if that sort of thing is going to be of long term advantage to the people of Ontario. I am going to suggest to the minister, and I am quite sure he would agree with me, that the same condition pertains in the old, historic provinces down by the sea. This sort of policy which is implicit in what Mr. Macaulay is suggesting is not of any value to them and it is not of value to us in western Canada. As a matter of fact, I know of no one in western Canada who needs a hippopotamus, and I do not know of anyone at the moment who wants one.
I think we need to adopt a policy based upon the promise of support from the most people in Canada. We know that in western Canada there are some industries who would find it to their advantage to have complete free trade tomorrow morning. I am going to say very frankly to you that those industries in western Canada know that they cannot have free trade tomorrow morning. At the same time, they cannot stand the backdoor preferences that have been brought in by the government in recent months. I am not going into the question of whether they were
3186	HOUSE OF
National Economic Development Board legal or illegal, but nevertheless there is protectionism being brought in. The minister has from time to time assured us that these protectionisms are for the short term; they are going to be removed.
I have another aspect of trade that I should like to bring forward, about which I am going to make suggestions to the minister later. I think that today we are dependent for the maintenance of the economy of Canada, to the extent of almost 30 per cent, upon our exports. I have found, in the last year for which I have figures, 1961, that of our total exports no less than 54.5 per cent went to the United States. In that same year, of our imports, no less than 67 per cent were brought in from the United States. The second most important trading nation to us is, of course, the mother country. In 1961, we sold, of our total exports, some 15.6 per cent to her and we brought back some 10.7 per cent of our total imports.
I made inquiry, too, about our trade relations that exist between Canada and the signatories of the treaty of Rome, in other words the members of the common market. I found, somewhat to my dismay, that of our total exports to those countries in 1961, only
8.4	per cent went to all the members of the common market. From them, we bought only
6.4	per cent of our total imports. When we add these figures together, both exports and imports, we realize that Canada is a north Atlantic trading nation, without any question. Our past experience having been in that direction, I think we may safely assume that our future is going to lie in that direction, too.
I have a criticism to make of the government at this time because, to the south of us, we have the President of the United States submitting to congress and successfully obtaining therefrom, legislation which was called the trade expansion act of 1962. We, on this side of the house, like to call it the trade liberalization act. This act gives to the president of the United States extraordinary powers to make agreements, not with one nation but with groups of nations such as the common market. Here, it seems to me, is a clear invitation to Canada to improve her position by making available to Canadians the export market containing 300 million people rather than the small market of 18 million people which we have at home. I think the government has been remiss because I am quite certain that this government has not pressed this matter with the President of the United States or with his secretary of commerce.
We go on attempting to purchase from the United States some $460 million to $480 million worth of goods more than we sell to


them. I do not believe it should be difficult for our leaders to impress upon the President of the United States and his secretary of commerce that Canada cannot go on interminably borrowing half a billion dollars in cash down there to buy goods from them, when there is this invitation to reduce tariffs. I want to ask this government, to ask the minister, to what extent they have gone to the United States and placed Canada's position before the United States. Have they said to them, certainly, we want to equate our balance, but we want to equate our balance with you not by going on buying imports to the extent of half a billion dollars, but by asking you to reduce your tariffs to the point where we can sell half a billion dollars worth of goods to you. It would seem to me that would be the positive approach and that would be the best way of taking the furrow out of the brow of the Minister of Labour annually in the wintertime when we seem, in Canada, to come to the position where employment is related to the condition of the equinox.
I find that many of the industries in which we have exports are the resources industries largely dealing with materials in their raw state. There is a totally inadequate and unhappy amount of Canadian labour content in those things we are selling. I find that in the automobile manufacturing industry in Canada today there is almost 10 per cent of the value of the automobile that is made up of labour. This, in Canada, is a fairly high percentage. In the case of the fruit and vegetable canning industry, the labour content is 10 per cent in relation to the total value of the manufactured goods. In so far as crude petroleum and natural gas is concerned, Mr. Chairman, do you know that the labour content is only 4 per cent of the total value of the goods sold?
Now, I am not going to disparage the labour that goes into the development aspect of that industry. This represents a tremendous expenditure of money.

speechtext:
Mr. Chairman, this is what I was attempting to do. I had no intention of quoting the whole article. This has to do with the long term measures which were proposed by the government in the throne speech, and certainly one of the long term measures we might expect is an effective economic development board. That is how the editorial is associated with it, but if the chairman and the committee desire me not to go further into the part where it deals with some of the faults it finds with the Liberal party, then I shall be quite happy to leave that particular part out. As it says in this editorial, there is no sign yet of the long term measures, and it was in that connection I gave the quotation from this national newspaper which has not been unfriendly to the government. This is a judgment of a reputable newspaper which I believe has the interests of Canada at heart. This is an editorial expression of the kind of concern for Canada that I myself had when earlier this session I said this:
It is not only this minority Conservative government's reputation that is at stake at this time ... but there is something of much greater importance about which I want to speak, although the government's reputation has a direct bearing on this other matter, and that is the question of the confidence of Canadians in the ability of our free parliamentary democracy to supply the answers and chart the course for the great social changes that are now under way in Canada.
Then I went on to speak of the government's apparent incapacity to understand the kind of social ferment and unrest that is bubbling away under the surface of our national life

and which occasionally manifests itself publicly in a number of undesirable ways. The gravest dangers to Canada's unity and economic independence lie in the months and immediate years ahead. No longer will any government be able to cap the well or hold back our people's aspirations by expedient grants, handouts or appointments in a piecemeal fashion. We are faced with a ground-swell of what I think of as a frustrated Canadian spirit that yearns for greatness for our country; that calls for Canada's sympathetic and helpful identification with the emerging nations; that desires deeply the respect of our traditional friends and neighbours; that wants to believe in political morality and the courage of conviction; that is struggling toward a proud and satisfying Canadian identity in the family of nations.
This failure by the government to "understand tomorrow", to borrow Rabbi Rosenberg's phrase, is what is holding this country back. This failure to understand tomorrow is what makes possible the rise of demagogues and tyrants, or maybe we are in the grip of them already. But we must do more than understand tomorrow. A government must have policies for Canada that prove they do understand tomorrow and know what is going on, and that they are capable of leading the country forward. For instance, where is the integrated, comprehensive policy that would make the C.N.R. a useful instrument in the economic recovery of Canada's depressed areas? As my colleague from Antigonish-Guysborough pointed out in his excellent speech on Thursday, December 6:
We all know that governments over the years have been concerned with this matter, and indeed went so far as to create a royal commission to look into it. The royal commission reported that by reason of the development of competition, particularly trucking competition, in central Canada the railways are having a tough time making ends meet in the extremities of the country. Consequently they apply for permission to raise their freight rates, but this permission they use to its full extent only in those extremities. Therefore the freight rates go up in the east and the west, and they are kept down in the centre of the country by reason of the competition there.
The royal commission on transportation points out:
While we recognize the complexity of the rate structure issue, we cannot help but believe that railway resistance to the adoption of a more cost-oriented basis for ratemaking is essentially unrealistic and reflects a degree of institutional rigidity which is out of place in the transportation environment of today.
Those are the words of the royal commission on transportation, and I use this example to illustrate the ridiculous situation where a publicly owned utility, owned and paid for by the Canadian taxpayer, operates in such a way as to prejudice the growth of secondary

industry in areas where such growth is of prime importance to the local taxpayer. All because of a lack of a nation-wide transportation policy we cut the economic throats of the very areas the government now says it is going to assist by setting up another board or council. I presume that this board will be working hard to counteract the penalizing policies of other boards, and all this costs money, hard earned taxpayers' money. Why spend all this money if it is not used in conjunction with a national policy designed to produce the Canada of tomorrow?
In these fast moving days we know that many airplanes-I believe we have learned this-are practically obsolete before they are off the drawing board. I submit that most of our piecemeal legislation is the same way. The basic problem is that all these bits and pieces of legislation only delay the full answer to our nation's needs because they are not connected to a national policy, and all hon. members know why. There is no national policy. There is no national policy on defence; there is no national policy on power and water resources; there is no national policy on depressed area redevelopment; there is no national policy on foreign investments in, and subsequent control of, Canadian resources and industries; there is no national policy on medical care, contributory portable pensions and other social security measures; there is no national policy on public housing.

If the government really means business, will it please now give this country an integrated over-all long range economic policy of national development which takes into account the urgent needs of municipalities and the small businessman, as well as our industrial complex. Will it please consolidate all its boards, commissions and development councils, which have been riding in six different directions at the same time, into one department of action for the economic growth of all regions of Canada, under a minister directly responsible to parliament, a minister available for questioning.

The municipal, national and international experts have all reported. Under this new act we are apparently now going to analyse the analysers. We are going to study their report on previous studies and reports. This is a waste of time and money.
The country is read for a policy of action that can save us our financial and political independence and achieve a rate of growth to lick unemployment and remove the immigration bars once more.
What is the government's reply to these auspicious circumstances? They say: "Let us run around the track once more. Let us have more studies and reports and recommendations." Can we not now move, or has our will and moral fibre deteriorated to the point where the government is biologically incapable of taking a strong firm decision on anything that requires a national policy.
The measure before us states that annual reports are to be submitted to the responsible minister three months after the close of each fiscal year. The government has all the information it requires right now to give the green light to the Minister of Finance to formulate a national development policy. Why wait any longer?

Mr. Chairman, we in this corner believe that there is a lot to be done, not only to establish a national economic development board, but also to develop our natural resources.

Yesterday, I attended meetings in the riding of Richelieu-Vercheres, a good solid Liberal riding for a number of years. I also was in the Shefford constituency where, in spite of a terrible storm, I met several thousand people.
I have also realized that the people of our counties, the average Canadians understand the problems, and especially their solutions, much more readily sometimes than certain members of parliament can or seem to.
In fact, when we ask the people of those constituencies: Is there in Canada a man or woman who is worrying about not being able to find tomorrow a dress, a topcoat or fur coat, a man's garment, a hat, in short, clothes, food or electric appliances? We get the following reply: Nobody stops to think about that, not even a single member of parliament.
There is only one question which comes to everybody's mind: Is our purchasing power sufficient for us to buy existing commodities in Canada, so that production in our country may be under the control of the Canadian people?
We must give more importance to the consumer than to the producer in Canada. Producers have but one problem, to sell their products. That is why a national economic development board which would encourage or control production in our country would in no way solve the problem. Members of parliament, like the rest of the people, must concern themselves with the problem of making it possible for consumers to buy the commodities manufactured by our producers or by the production complex in Canada.
Naturally, some hon. members and some economists will claim that that will bring inflation, that it is utopian, just like certain writers and economists who maintain that Social Credit is a utopia. Those who do not know what the word "utopia" means-and that includes several members of parliament-like to say: "It's a top; it's a top; it's a top."
Mr. Chairman, Social Crediters have a solution to offer to Canada. Not only do they offer an answer to Canada, but it is the true reason why we are assembled here and why the whole country should present today a united front, and act and exist as a single person.
Social Credit will not perform miracles.
Besides, the Liberals have never performed any, far from it. They created problems so that we could perform miracles afterwards.
National Economic Development Board
The Conservatives have not done much more in the last few years. Social Crediters do not pretend to be supermen, but they do claim that they can bring to Canada an answer likely to arouse interest, not only within our boundaries, but also outside the country.
If this economic development board now under discussion has not yet been set up, it is through the fault of the Liberals, even though they complain-as can be seen in the press-that the government has not accomplished anything since it came into power.
All rushed forward for the onslaught. Of course one can make a few suggestions concerning the national economic development board. But what practical ideas did the Liberals put forward in answer to the Conservative program? In this instance, we see quite clearly, once more, that both parties are of the same essence, that they have the same organization, an identical platform, the same fundamental principles.
Mr. Chairman, I do not propose to detain the house any longer. If the national economic development board is important to Canada and to the hon. members, let us by all means enact the bill, create that board, and ask it to create in turn the economic conditions which will-or so Canadians hope -lay the foundation for economic development.

Mr. Chairman, this discussion has proceeded for some considerable time, but there are one or two things I want to say on behalf of the New Democratic party. There has certainly been widespread interest in the bill we are considering at the present moment to establish a national economic development board. The reason is that people are asking, is it possible to manage and direct the development of our Canadian economy so as to correct the weaknesses which have been apparent for many years to anyone with eyes to see and ears to hear? The bill might very well be called "Great Expectations", because I suggest that people are expecting great things from it. But they will be disappointed and disillusioned unless the government is wise enough to accept many of the carefully considered amendments which will be proposed by my colleagues in this corner of the house.
I submit, Mr. Chairman, that the success of this bill will depend on at least four things: first, an understanding of the problems to be solved; second, the sincerity of the government in promoting the concept of modern planning; third, the composition and
3192	HOUSE OF
National Economic Development Board competence of the board to be appointed; fourth, and probably the most important of all, the courage to implement the recommendations of the board both in the public and the private areas of our economy.
The week before this session opened last September there was an editorial in Maclean's magazine by Peter Newman, one of the most experienced and respected commentators in the newspaper field in Canada. Now, sir, I am not going to read the whole editorial, but I do crave your indulgence to read a few paragraphs which deal directly with the problem that is before us this evening. After referring to the stopgap measures adopted by this government last summer Mr. Newman continued as follows;
The cardinal task facing us now is to correct this flabby approach to economic problems. We need, first, a measure of economic planning to bring direction and purpose to the management of the nation's affairs. Economic planning in one form or another is the means by which the western European democracies have outdistanced us economically. Administrators in Washington are using-under other names-many of the methods that together make up economic planning. Ottawa is not; but sooner or later Ottawa is going to have to start...
The vital first step in the intellectual reorientation the new economic climate demands is to throw off the tyranny of words. In the past the phrase "economic planning" has been damned as socialistic doctrine-
Mr. Chairman, I recall, as has already been mentioned in this debate, that in introducing this legislation the Minister of Finance very carefully, but I think very foolishly, avoided using the word "planning" at any time. May I continue;
A planned economy does not signify state control. Rather, it is the deliberate use of those methods that can encourage government, industry and labour to co-operate voluntarily-
Until recently, most economists tended to recognize only two earlier models: the totalitarian model of Russia, and the unrestricted free enterprise model of the United States. But as Robert Fowlerto whom reference has already been made by the hon. member for Vancouver South this evening-
-the enlightened executive who heads the Canadian Pulp and Paper Association has recently been pointing out, the experience of Europe now offers us a third alternative: the choice of a free but planned economy. "To adapt this to Canada," Fowler admits, "will require profound changes in our attitudes and our laws... but it may offer the best chance of restoring rapid economic growth in this country, and a chance of achieving a distinctive national identity."
Briefly, sir, may I indicate a number of factors which merit consideration in setting up this board. First, the final purpose must be to assure the development and use of our material and human resources to the highest degree possible in the service of people here and elsewhere. Second, both private and


public sectors of the economy must play a part in any effective plan. Third, long range objectives should be established as this is not intended to meet a temporary emergency. It will be a continuing process. Fourth, the whole of Canada must be involved, not just a few isolated areas that may be particularly in difficulty at the present time. Fifth, the best available personnel should be engaged. During the war the late C. D. Howe did this successfully to prepare Canada for its war contribution. Surely we can do as well in peacetime. Sixth, co-operation of all sections of the community will be the key to the eventual success of this legislation. I am thinking at this point not just of industry, labour and government but of people generally.
I submit that if the board that will be appointed and which will be responsible for this legislation is wise it will consider the importance of this factor, that working people of all kinds need to participate more in our Canadian democracy. We need men and women from management and the unions and the civil service certainly but also from the universities, consumer groups and citizen organizations across the country.
In this age of bigness ordinary people become divorced from the end product, the results of their labours. Not only in the interests of democracy but in the interest of good mental health men and women need to be consulted more and trusted more in the management of the country's affairs. After all, this is their business. Given an opportunity to participate, Canadians would respond to a peacetime adventure of this kind with the same spirit that has always characterized our people whenever they have faced challenging problems ever since confederation, almost 100 years ago.

I suggest, sir, that it is, and it always has been, difficult ever since 1867 to maintain a viable, dynamic, growing economy in this country. It has always required planning. It has never resulted from the operation of simple laissez faire; never at any time, and whenever any attempt has been made to leave it to the so-called natural forces, the economy has flagged. So far as I can see, that has been true in the nineteenth century and in the twentieth century as well. Plans were made for the transformation of the Canadian economy from a wartime to a peacetime basis. We had a formidable task at that time. There were one million men and women under arms and there were another million working in munitions plants. Hon. gentlemen will recall, some who have been here a long time like the hon. member for Winnipeg North Centre, that he and his friends expected a depression at that time. I suggest that one of the principal reasons there was not a depression was precisely because there was intelligent, broad planning of the kind that was carried on at that time by the government of that day.
This is precisely what this country needs now, and it is precisely what we recommended in the last election campaign. I could read from the program that we put forward. I remember the scorn that was poured upon these proposals of ours, particularly by the Minister of Labour. We have had these statements brought up before in this debate, and I am not going to repeat them. The minister will recall, himself, how he dismissed all this planning. This debate has gone on for some considerable time and as I said, on the whole- and I emphasize on the whole with one or two noticeable exceptions, some of which we have seen tonight-it has been orderly and constructive. I appreciate the manner in which hon. members from all parties participated, despite the fact that we have varying points of view in looking upon the problem. Like everyone else, everyone is for virtue and everyone is against sin, but when it comes to describe what is virtue and what is sin sometimes there are differences of opinion.
Sometimes we have hon. members saying we should have planning of a mandatory nature, and that term is more than suggestive and more than indicative; but our friends in the New Democratic party have expressed that point of view, have expressed it forcefully, and from their own point of view have

National Economic Development Board expressed it very well. It will not surprise them at all when I tell them I disagree with the point of view they express because it is not reconcilable with a free economy, and so far as the government is concerned we believe in that system despite the fact that in historical connotations and in our growth there have been some limitations on the development of the nation in a free enterprise system.
Some hon. members have said that the board is inadequate. There have been suggestions that the board is going to consist of only one man. Other inferences have been drawn, I think honestly drawn, and as we go on to deal with the clauses I shall deal with them in greater length.
The chairman is to be a full time chairman and a varying number has been set for the members. They are not frozen into a compact group. In fact there is a certain amount of elasticity whereby within this number we can have a board representative of industry, agriculture and all the various groups in this great nation. It is true membership is of a voluntary nature. Members will be paid their expenses. They will not be paid salaries per se; but, Mr. Chairman, you will notice that under clause 16 the board may appoint such officers as it requires and these will not be employed through the civil service commission. They will be appointed by the board and they will be paid such salaries as the board shall determine.
There is no question as to why that provision has been included. I may say I expect to be here when this bill is implemented, and if this provision carries I hope we will attract to the board the very best brains obtainable in Canada for its service, regardless of politics and regardless of anything else. With all due respect I might as well face this problem frankly. If we limit this board to retaining employees under the civil service commission then I point out that the statutory salaries which are fixed will apply and the statutory competitions must be held.
I have had something to do with the drafting of this bill and I resent any inferences to gray eminences. Any gray eminence who exists, when he found out about this board he found out about it from me. That is the first he heard about it and I am determined, so long as I am Minister of Finance and so long as I have responsibility for handling this bill, or act when it becomes statutory legislation, that we will have a group of employees, servants-call them what you will-associated with the board-

They will not be bureaucrats, I can assure you on that. We inherited a lot of bureaucrats and bureaucrats have their place, and I must say they are right there.
Somebody said "You have enough men now to advise you." That is true in the civil service. We have, I suggest, as able a group of men and women in the upper echelons of the civil service as any country in the world, and I pay tribute to them; but they are very, very limited in number and the problems are very, very many. Virtually all of them in the civil service are saddled with responsibilities of administration, departmental administration and day to day problems. They can deal with those day to day problems and they deal with them effectively, certainly to my satisfaction and the satisfaction of my colleagues. Though we all make mistakes, on the whole they deal with their work reasonably well; but when it comes to the long term problems they just have not the time to give their attention to those problems. Certainly hon. gentlemen opposite who have experience in administration know the problems they are confronted with from day to day. Our senior civil servants are not in the position to deal with these long range problems as they should. When some of us-shall I say, "when I" looked over the situation and I realized the long term problems that had to be solved, and I realized the problem of the balance of payments, I realized that we had to have a group associated with this government; not, as the hon. member for Davenport said the other night, a wing or part of the Department of Finance. It will not be a part of the Department of Finance. It will be an independent board entirely, reporting to the Minister of Finance, whoever he happens to be at the moment, but it will be no more a part of the Department of Finance than is the tariff board or any similar body. It will be an independent board to which we hope to invite in a voluntary capacity the leaders of business, agriculture and labour, with all the groups in this country sitting around. Somebody said it would be a cocktail party. That was said by my genial friend down to the right, with his brilliant tongue but not always the logical reasoning that one would expect from him. He is the one who referred to this board as being a cocktail party. I am told, without any great knowledge of it, Mr. Chairman, that sometimes good things emanate even from cocktail parties. But certainly it is not a cocktail party that is going to determine the work of this board. There will be groups associated with it comprising, I hope-as I have said-the very best brains this country can produce, men and women in economics and finance and experienced in the various problems with which we are confronted. We are also asking the universities to help. We are asking them

to solve certain problems by delegating to them, or some industrial research group, certain problems.
There are no other problems, Mr. Chairman. This country and this parliament needs the support of all parties here to make sure that the type of men and women we invite to come to this board, the type of men and women the board after it is appointed will retain and ask to take employment here, will be of the calibre that the nation needs. In the face of this we have picayune, partisan criticism such as has emanated from two or three speeches, and only two or three, to the effect that it is going to be very difficult to get the men and women that I hope will be attracted to this board and who I believe can be attracted to the board if this parliament deals with the bill as I suggested, with all respect, it should be dealt with.
I am not going to go into all the criticisms which have been uttered by various hon. members during the debate. As I said, Mr. Chairman, I think most of them have been on a very high level. One could spend a great deal of time dealing with them, but I would hope this committee could see its way clear at least to pass clause 1 this evening in order to get off the first clause, and then we will deal with the details of the other clauses as time goes on.
I have notes of all the comments of every hon. member except those who have spoken this evening. I did not have the time to make notes of what was said in those speeches this evening. The hon. member for Coast-Capilano said that the board should report to a committee of three ministers. I do not think anyone expects a board to report to a group of ministers. It must report to somebody who is responsible for it, and there certainly is no difficulty in the world about setting up-as my hon. friend for Bonavista-Twillingate and others who have been in government know-a committee of the ministry to deal with specific problems as they develop.
The hon. member for Red Deer made an address earlier in the debate, I think when we were at the resolution stage, in which he suggested that a great deal of this work should have been delegated to the productivity council, and we did not need this board at all. That is an argument which he advanced and I think there are others who perhaps share his view. I would point out to the hon. member that the United Kingdom has had a productivity council for many years and it has done very, very good work, as has the productivity council in this country. But in the United Kingdom two years ago they also set up what is popularly called Neddy,
National Economic Development Board the national economic development-I do not know what that last initial stands for-

speechtext:
Well, Mr. Chairman, east is east and west is west, and never the twain shall meet. Apparently the hon. member for Red Deer wants to incorporate the two groups. We are following the example set by the United Kingdom in setting up a national economic development board which will work very, very closely in co-operation with the productivity council. A great deal has been said with respect to planning. Some of it has been said by our friends in the New Democratic party. My hon. friend from Essex East and others have referred to the great development that has taken place in western Europe. They referred to France as an example, Sweden and other countries. Certainly we in this country who study these matters would be the first to admit that they have made tremendous advances and tremendous development has taken place. However, I would suggest that this committee must not overlook the constitutional problems with which we are faced; the fact that this is a federal state, that we have provinces and are not a unitary state, that property and civil rights impinge upon trade and commerce and there are always constitutional problems which do not apply to unitary states such as -I am not sure of the constitutional developments of all the European countries and I do not want to be caught out in this connection, but I would suggest France, Sweden, Belgium, Switzerland and the United Kingdom. Also, we certainly have not the government control or the intervention of the state in this country; and, with all due respect to my hon. friends in the far corner, I do not expect we will have such control for some time such as there is in France, Sweden and other European countries.
We are developing here a pattern which is somewhat different from that which is applied in western Europe. I think it is closely analogous to that which applies in the United
3198	HOUSE OF
National Economic Development Board Kingdom and it is one which I think will result in a great deal of development and planning in this country. It is easy to say, "Ah, it is only a shell, only an empty gesture. It does not mean anything at all". Those comments can be made and have been made to some extent during this debate. I disagree with them positively and absolutely. As I said earlier, I know what is the concept of planning, not the mandatory planning that some would have, but the long range planning which I and my colleagues had in mind when we asked this parliament to set up this board. It is far from perfect. No organization can be perfect and no organization will be perfect. It is going to face difficulties, of course. There are many problems which we have to face. There are problems such as the hon. member for Vancouver South referred to this evening. There is this problem, for instance. My hon. friend from Vancouver South said, "Well, after all President Kennedy now has his long term trading bill. Why do you not approach him and enter trade negotiations? Why do you not arrange for reciprocal trade or break down the barriers between our country and the United States?" That, of course, is an argument which has been advanced before and it is one worthy of comment. But certainly President Kennedy made it abundantly clear, I hope, that any concessions that he makes so far as tariffs are concerned are going to be on the most favoured nation basis, and when he makes reductions they are going to apply to all the nations that come into the most favoured nation tariffs. Much as we have pride in Canada and admire our friends in the United States, I would think that if the hon. member for Vancouver South were in charge of tariff negotiations for the United States he might hesitate in making too many concessions to Canada. I know they would apply to the whole world, but they still have to trade and negotiate with the United Kingdom. These matters however to a large extent depend upon a certain gentleman across the channel, as to whether the United Kingdom enters the common market and whether they deal with the United Kingdom or the common market countries generally. There are, of course, problems confronting us, and that is one. We have the balance of payments situation. We have the tariff negotiations. We have all these things to which hon. members have referred. I suggest that having had a debate which has gone on, now, for some days-and I am glad it has, because it has been, as I said, a very good debate-perhaps we could proceed. I understand there are to be some suggestions made, some amendments which hon. members would like to move. I should like to hear these proposals and give careful consideration to them.


There is, on our part, no fixation with regard to this measure. There is nothing in this on which we stand or fall, come what may. It is a bill which has been drafted and to which consideration has been given by many people.
I am prepared to listen to any argument which may be put forward from time to time and, if I can see my way clear, to accept it if it does not involve the principle upon which the bill is based. I know of one proposal which is coming forward. It is a proposal I should like to debate strongly, because I think the type of man we should bring in has to be assured of relative continuity of employment, and this assurance cannot be given if he is only appointed for a short term. But that is another matter, and, as I say, I hope the committee can see its way to make progress before it rises at ten o'clock.
We read in the papers from time to time that this parliament may not be here for very long-that there may be an election. There are various predictions made which, perhaps, are products of the imagination. Nevertheless, these are considerations which we should have in mind. Therefore I should like to see this clause passed so that we may go on tomorrow and make further progress. So, if in its wisdom parliament decides that there should be other issues resolved in another form, we should at least have this bill through and begin acquiring the personnel to man the board. I can assure this committee that when the announcement of the appointment is made by this government we shall hear from all sides that we have chosen wisely and well. I am sure that this would also be true if another government were making the appointment. Unless such a choice can be made, a choice will not be made. That is why I should like to have this clause agreed to, and deal with it.

However, I do have one idea I want to discuss and I insist I do so very seriously. In the bill we find under duties and powers a clause which reads:
The achievement of the highest possible level of efficient production and employment so as to ensure the raising of standards of living in all parts of Canada.
That phrase "in all parts of Canada" is the matter I propose to deal with this evening.
I could preface these remarks in no better terms than those used by my colleague from Toronto Davenport on November 29 as reported in Hansard on page 2147.
These were the third and fourth points he made.
Third, this council should be concerned not only with analysing economic trends; it should also have as one of its main functions responsibility for working out solutions to our basic problems in practical terms. This means that the council should translate a good rate of economic growth into targets for each of the principal industries of the country; and in doing this it would be necessary to take into account regional problems and regional points of view. Fourth, the council should point the fact out to the government if it appears that any of the government's policies are in conflict with one another, as recently they have so often been, and it should be its responsibility to suggest how these conflicts might be reconciled.
