speechtext:
If hon. gentlemen opposite want to interrupt, my remarks will take that much more time. It is entirely up to them. I intend to have my say whether they like it or not.
I want to develop that idea a little further. In a country such as ours, national goals should not be set without due regard for the development of each region in Canada. This means, in effect, that planning will and must require a regional as well as a national approach. If we look at our geographical areas and go back to our historical methods we shall see clearly the great need of the regional approach. Our national concerns, by which I mean our business enterprises, our national business organizations, whether they be public or private, may at times make decisions
which in their minds appear to be sound economics. But too often these decisions, even when they are correct in a narrow economic sense for a particular industry, result in a harmful dislocation in a particular region. In the end this can only work to the detriment of the national interest. The best example, of course, is our national communication system but there are other industries which have advanced the argument of economics as justification for concentrating in. one area or another. In many cases it is doubtful if there really was justification for this concentration. The Trans-Canada Air Lines case is one instance of this. The transfer from east to west was based on the advantages of more economic operation, we are told. This is at least questionable in this particular case if all facts are taken into consideration-the piecemeal moves, the additional competition of air lines, the day to day decisions taken without regard for over-all effect. When all these things are taken into consideration it is doubtful if the regional development or, indeed, the national interest, have been well served by this move. Many of us contend they have not. A shift seems to have taken place from decentralization in recent times. I cannot express it better than did my colleague from Toronto Davenport whom I quoted earlier.
As far as our western problems are concerned, we have reached a stage where much thought and study is required. Matters have reached a point at which a complete re-examination of our financial and economic position within confederation is needed. The application of the Rowell-Sirois commission recommendations served well in their time. But when it came to the time where adjustments were required the present government saw fit simply to scrap them. This needs to be taken up again. Such a council as proposed here should be able to work with such other bodies as are established from time to time for the purpose of re-examining our constitutional or other relationships. This is not said lightly. We have had dislocations in the past and we may well have them again. Western Canada cannot long continue to expend its efforts to develop its industries only to find that almost as soon as they are developed and established they are whisked from under their nose for establishment elsewhere. Our trade and economic structures have long been designed to work in favour of the more industrialized centres. This is the kind of problem, among others, which a council of this nature should be designed to solve.
Industrial development, economic growth and expanding trade should be viewed and
3200	HOUSE OF
National Economic Development Board encouraged so as to provide benefit to all regions of our country. If our national life is to be maintained in a healthy, vigorous condition we must make sure that our maritime as well as our prairie provinces share in our objective of an ever-rising standard of living, and I suggest the minister has a great deal of knowledge of that question.
The exploitation of the tremendous wealth of our western provinces is not developing at a pace consistent with our capabilities because we are handicapped in so many ways. Population is one, the tendency to centralization of many of our major industries, both private and public, is another. This requires the setting of regional as well as national goals, and national goals should be adjusted to benefit regional development. The establishment of large concerns in the industrial east, often behind tariff protection, should not be permitted adversely to affect regional industries, in some cases even to destroy them. This has too often been the case. We are not here pleading for special privileges but only for an opportunity to develop at the same rate as the country as a whole.
A national economic development board, with this kind of objective and with the means at its disposal to plan, to analyse and to recommend forcibly, can and should be an instrument for a really great step forward and for sustained progress in our economic life.

Mr. Chairman, I hope the house will allow me to make a few brief remarks on the bill before us.
In the speech from the throne at the opening of parliament, we had the privilege of learning that the government was committed to bring before the house a program of legislation meant in part to stimulate the Canadian economy and to maintain a high level of employment.
The national economic development board, and this will come as a surprise to many, since the Conservative party have traditionally held that the idea of a planned economy was dangerous.
During the course of this debate, we have been reminded of the heated opposition raised by the supporters of this government when a similar bill was submitted to the house some years ago. Such a change of heart is not easily explained. There can be only one conclusion and it is that the government, having failed to solve Canada's economic problems through policies originating from within, must now rely on a solution suggested by the Liberal opposition. Of course, Mr. Chairman, I would not like to give the impression that I find fault with a government borrowing suggestions from other political parties for its legislation if they can be a real contribution to the welfare of the nation. If, after opposing a project because it was based on planning, the government decides today to reverse its policy and to sponsor an absolutely similar project, we must welcome that.
In fact, I find a little ridiculous the prudish reserve with which some people will approach the word or the idea of planning. In a country such as ours, where the government interferes in almost all fields of national activities, where almost one third of all revenues are handed back to the government in the form of taxes, where the government has taken under its control a large part of the production and consumption system, how could it be possible to solve the inevitable

problems of such a complex economy without planning through state intervention?
If a charge is to be laid against the government, it is for not having set up this development board a long time ago. It is obvious that in order to ensure the rational and fair development of the whole country, guidance must come from the central authority.
One of the most loathesome aspects of the present unemployment crisis in Canada is the fact that this social evil seriously affects some regions of the country, whereas in others there is almost full employment and a measure of prosperity. That is where guided development could help the regions hardest hit by unemployment and business stagnation. (Text):
